# Monte Carlo verification of the analytical power calculation
# Simulating data from the compound symmetry structure

set.seed(42)

# Parameters
mu1 <- 51
mu2 <- 49
sigma_marginal <- 2.5
k <- 3
rho <- 0.5
alpha <- 0.05
n_per_group <- 18
n_sim <- 5000

# Compound symmetry covariance matrix
# Σ = σ² [(1-ρ)I + ρ11ᵀ]
Sigma <- sigma_marginal^2 * ((1 - rho) * diag(k) + rho * matrix(1, k, k))

cat("Monte Carlo Simulation Verification\n")
cat("====================================\n")
cat(sprintf("Sample size per group: %d\n", n_per_group))
cat(sprintf("Number of simulations: %d\n", n_sim))
cat(sprintf("Significance level (two-sided): %.3f\n", alpha))
cat(sprintf("Random seed: 42\n\n")

cat("Compound Symmetry Covariance Matrix:\n")
print(round(Sigma, 4))
cat("\n")

# Simulate data and perform tests
rejection_count <- 0

for (sim in 1:n_sim) {
  # Generate data for group 1
  Y1 <- matrix(rnorm(n_per_group * k, mean = mu1), nrow = n_per_group, ncol = k)
  # Apply correlation structure via Cholesky decomposition
  L <- chol(Sigma)
  Y1 <- matrix(rnorm(n_per_group * k), nrow = n_per_group, ncol = k) %*% L + mu1
  
  # Generate data for group 2
  Y2 <- matrix(rnorm(n_per_group * k, mean = mu2), nrow = n_per_group, ncol = k)
  L <- chol(Sigma)
  Y2 <- matrix(rnorm(n_per_group * k), nrow = n_per_group, ncol = k) %*% L + mu2
  
  # Compute subject-level averages
  avg1 <- rowMeans(Y1)
  avg2 <- rowMeans(Y2)
  
  # Perform two-sample t-test on subject averages
  t_result <- t.test(avg1, avg2, var.equal = TRUE)
  p_value <- t_result$p.value
  
  if (p_value < alpha) {
    rejection_count <- rejection_count + 1
  }
}

mc_power <- rejection_count / n_sim
mc_se <- sqrt(mc_power * (1 - mc_power) / n_sim)
ci_lower <- mc_power - 1.96 * mc_se
ci_upper <- mc_power + 1.96 * mc_se

cat("Monte Carlo Results (n=18 per group):\n")
cat("====================================\n")
cat(sprintf("Simulations: %d\n", n_sim))
cat(sprintf("Rejections: %d\n", rejection_count))
cat(sprintf("Empirical Power: %.6f\n", mc_power))
cat(sprintf("Monte Carlo SE: %.6f\n", mc_se))
cat(sprintf("95%% CI: [%.6f, %.6f]\n\n", ci_lower, ci_upper))

# Compare to analytical result
analytical_power <- 0.814738
cat(sprintf("Analytical Power (n=18): %.6f\n", analytical_power))
cat(sprintf("Difference: %.6f\n", abs(mc_power - analytical_power)))

plan.estimand: Between-group mean difference on subject-level average across 3 repeated measurements
plan.hypothesis: Group 1 mean (51) differs from Group 2 mean (49) on the repeated-measures average
assumptions: Multivariate normal observations
Compound symmetry covariance structure
No missing data
No group-by-time interaction
Balanced design with equal allocation to groups
Homogeneous variance and correlation structure across groups
Sphericity holds (equivalent to compound symmetry)
Subject-level average used as the test statistic
Pooled t-test (equivalent to between-group F) on averaged outcome
scientific_notes: Compound symmetry implies constant correlation ρ=0.5 between all pairs of repeated measurements
The effective variance of the subject-level average Y̅ᵢ is Var(Y̅ᵢ) = σ²(1 + (k-1)ρ)/k where σ²=2.5², k=3, ρ=0.5
Effect size Δ = μ₁ - μ₂ = 51 - 49 = 2 on the original scale
The pooled t-test on subject averages has standard error based on the averaged variance within and between groups
Two-sided test at α=0.05 requires inverting the two-sample t test for minimum n per group achieving 80% power

# Repeated-measures ANOVA: Between-group power calculation
# Design: Two groups, 3 repeated measurements, balanced allocation
# Testing: Subject-level average via pooled t-test (equivalent to between-group F)

library(tidyverse)
library(nlme)  # For flexible covariance structures

# Parameters
mu1 <- 51                    # Group 1 mean
mu2 <- 49                    # Group 2 mean
delta <- mu1 - mu2           # Effect size = 2
sigma_marginal <- 2.5        # Marginal SD at each occasion
k <- 3                       # Number of repeated measurements
rho <- 0.5                   # Compound symmetry correlation
alpha <- 0.05                # Significance level (two-sided)
target_power <- 0.80         # Target power

# Calculate effective variance of the subject-level average under compound symmetry
# Var(Y̅ᵢ) = σ²(1 + (k-1)ρ)/k
effective_var <- sigma_marginal^2 * (1 + (k - 1) * rho) / k
effective_sd <- sqrt(effective_var)

cat("Repeated-Measures ANOVA Analysis\n")
cat("==================================\n")
cat(sprintf("Group 1 mean (μ₁): %.2f\n", mu1))
cat(sprintf("Group 2 mean (μ₂): %.2f\n", mu2))
cat(sprintf("Effect size (Δ = μ₁ - μ₂): %.2f\n", delta))
cat(sprintf("\nMarginal SD at each occasion: %.2f\n", sigma_marginal))
cat(sprintf("Number of repeated measurements: %d\n", k))
cat(sprintf("Compound symmetry correlation (ρ): %.2f\n", rho))
cat(sprintf("\nEffective variance of subject-level average:\n"))
cat(sprintf("  Var(Y̅ᵢ) = σ²(1 + (k-1)ρ)/k = %.4f² × (1 + %d × %.2f) / %d\n", 
            sigma_marginal, k-1, rho, k))
cat(sprintf("         = %.4f × %.2f / %d\n", sigma_marginal^2, 1 + (k-1)*rho, k))
cat(sprintf("         = %.4f\n", effective_var))
cat(sprintf("Effective SD of subject-level average: %.4f\n\n", effective_sd))

# For a two-sample t-test on subject averages:
# The test statistic is t = (Ȳ₁ - Ȳ₂) / SE where
# SE = effective_sd × sqrt(2/n) for equal group sizes n
# 
# This is equivalent to testing the between-group effect in repeated-measures ANOVA
# using subject-level averages

# Critical value for two-sided test with df ≈ 2n - 2
t_crit_approx <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df = 100)  # approximate for larger n
cat(sprintf("Two-sided critical value (two-tailed, α=%.3f): ±%.4f\n\n", alpha, t_crit_approx))

# Function to calculate power for a given sample size per group
calculate_power <- function(n_per_group) {
  df <- 2 * n_per_group - 2
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df = df)
  se <- effective_sd * sqrt(2 / n_per_group)
  ncp <- delta / se  # Non-centrality parameter
  power <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df, ncp) + pt(-t_crit, df, ncp)
  return(power)
}

# Search for minimum sample size achieving target power
# Start with a reasonable guess
n_candidates <- seq(5, 100, by = 1)
powers <- sapply(n_candidates, calculate_power)

# Find the minimum n where power >= 0.80
minimum_n <- min(n_candidates[powers >= target_power])
power_at_min <- calculate_power(minimum_n)
power_at_prev <- calculate_power(minimum_n - 1)

cat("Sample Size Search Results:\n")
cat("============================\n")
cat(sprintf("Minimum participants per group: %d\n", minimum_n))
cat(sprintf("Achieved power at n=%d: %.6f\n", minimum_n, power_at_min))
cat(sprintf("Power at preceding design (n=%d): %.6f\n\n", minimum_n - 1, power_at_prev))

# Display a range of results for verification
cat("Power Analysis Table:\n")
cat("n\tPower\n")
for (n in seq(minimum_n - 3, minimum_n + 2)) {
  if (n > 0) {
    p <- calculate_power(n)
    cat(sprintf("%d\t%.6f\n", n, p))
  }
}

# Store final results for POWER_AGENT_RESULT
result_n <- minimum_n
result_power <- power_at_min

cat("\n\nFinal Result:\n")
cat(sprintf("Minimum sample size: %d participants per group\n", result_n))
cat(sprintf("Achieved power: %.6f\n", result_power))

cat(sprintf("         = %.4f × %.2f / %d\n", sigma_marginal^2, 1 + (k-1)*rho, k))
cat(sprintf("         = %.4f\n", effective_var))
cat(sprintf("Effective SD of subject-level average: %.4f\n\n", effective_sd))

# For a two-sample t-test on subject averages:
# The test statistic is t = (Ȳ₁ - Ȳ₂) / SE where
# SE = effective_sd × sqrt(2/n) for equal group sizes n
# 
# This is equivalent to testing the between-group effect in repeated-measures ANOVA
# using subject-level averages

# Critical value for two-sided test with df ≈ 2n - 2
t_crit_approx <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df = 100)  # approximate for larger n
cat(sprintf("Two-sided critical value (two-tailed, α=%.3f): ±%.4f\n\n", alpha, t_crit_approx))

# Function to calculate power for a given sample size per group
calculate_power <- function(n_per_group) {
  df <- 2 * n_per_group - 2
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df = df)
  se <- effective_sd * sqrt(2 / n_per_group)
  ncp <- delta / se  # Non-centrality parameter
  power <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df, ncp) + pt(-t_crit, df, ncp)
  return(power)
}

# Search for minimum sample size achieving target power
# Start with a reasonable guess
n_candidates <- seq(5, 100, by = 1)
powers <- sapply(n_candidates, calculate_power)

# Find the minimum n where power >= 0.80
minimum_n <- min(n_candidates[powers >= target_power])
power_at_min <- calculate_power(minimum_n)
power_at_prev <- calculate_power(minimum_n - 1)

cat("Sample Size Search Results:\n")
cat("============================\n")
cat(sprintf("Minimum participants per group: %d\n", minimum_n))
cat(sprintf("Achieved power at n=%d: %.6f\n", minimum_n, power_at_min))
cat(sprintf("Power at preceding design (n=%d): %.6f\n\n", minimum_n - 1, power_at_prev))

# Display a range of results for verification
cat("Power Analysis Table:\n")
cat("n\tPower\n")
for (n in seq(minimum_n - 3, minimum_n + 2)) {
  if (n > 0) {
    p <- calculate_power(n)
    cat(sprintf("%d\t%.6f\n", n, p))
  }
}

# Store final results for POWER_AGENT_RESULT
result_n <- minimum_n
result_power <- power_at_min

cat("\n\nFinal Result:\n")
cat(sprintf("Minimum sample size: %d participants per group\n", result_n))
cat(sprintf("Achieved power: %.6f\n", result_power))

# Monte Carlo verification of the analytical power calculation
# Simulating data from the compound symmetry structure

set.seed(42)

# Parameters
mu1 <- 51
mu2 <- 49
sigma_marginal <- 2.5
k <- 3
rho <- 0.5
alpha <- 0.05
n_per_group <- 18
n_sim <- 5000

# Compound symmetry covariance matrix
# Σ = σ² [(1-ρ)I + ρ11ᵀ]
Sigma <- sigma_marginal^2 * ((1 - rho) * diag(k) + rho * matrix(1, k, k))

cat("Monte Carlo Simulation Verification\n")
cat("====================================\n")
cat(sprintf("Sample size per group: %d\n", n_per_group))
cat(sprintf("Number of simulations: %d\n", n_sim))
cat(sprintf("Significance level (two-sided): %.3f\n", alpha))
cat(sprintf("Random seed: 42\n\n")

cat("Compound Symmetry Covariance Matrix:\n")
print(round(Sigma, 4))
cat("\n")

# Simulate data and perform tests
rejection_count <- 0

for (sim in 1:n_sim) {
  # Generate data for group 1
  Y1 <- matrix(rnorm(n_per_group * k, mean = mu1), nrow = n_per_group, ncol = k)
  # Apply correlation structure via Cholesky decomposition
  L <- chol(Sigma)
  Y1 <- matrix(rnorm(n_per_group * k), nrow = n_per_group, ncol = k) %*% L + mu1
  
  # Generate data for group 2
  Y2 <- matrix(rnorm(n_per_group * k, mean = mu2), nrow = n_per_group, ncol = k)
  L <- chol(Sigma)
  Y2 <- matrix(rnorm(n_per_group * k), nrow = n_per_group, ncol = k) %*% L + mu2
  
  # Compute subject-level averages
  avg1 <- rowMeans(Y1)
  avg2 <- rowMeans(Y2)
  
  # Perform two-sample t-test on subject averages
  t_result <- t.test(avg1, avg2, var.equal = TRUE)
  p_value <- t_result$p.value
  
  if (p_value < alpha) {
    rejection_count <- rejection_count + 1
  }
}

mc_power <- rejection_count / n_sim
mc_se <- sqrt(mc_power * (1 - mc_power) / n_sim)
ci_lower <- mc_power - 1.96 * mc_se
ci_upper <- mc_power + 1.96 * mc_se

cat("Monte Carlo Results (n=18 per group):\n")
cat("====================================\n")
cat(sprintf("Simulations: %d\n", n_sim))
cat(sprintf("Rejections: %d\n", rejection_count))
cat(sprintf("Empirical Power: %.6f\n", mc_power))
cat(sprintf("Monte Carlo SE: %.6f\n", mc_se))
cat(sprintf("95%% CI: [%.6f, %.6f]\n\n", ci_lower, ci_upper))

analytical_power <- 0.814738
cat(sprintf("Analytical Power (n=18): %.6f\n", analytical_power))

# Evidence e1; success=false

# Repeated-measures ANOVA: Between-group power calculation
# Design: Two groups, 3 repeated measurements, balanced allocation
# Testing: Subject-level average via pooled t-test (equivalent to between-group F)

library(tidyverse)
library(nlme)  # For flexible covariance structures

# Parameters
mu1 <- 51                    # Group 1 mean
mu2 <- 49                    # Group 2 mean
delta <- mu1 - mu2           # Effect size = 2
sigma_marginal <- 2.5        # Marginal SD at each occasion
k <- 3                       # Number of repeated measurements
rho <- 0.5                   # Compound symmetry correlation
alpha <- 0.05                # Significance level (two-sided)
target_power <- 0.80         # Target power

# Calculate effective variance of the subject-level average under compound symmetry
# Var(Y̅ᵢ) = σ²(1 + (k-1)ρ)/k
effective_var <- sigma_marginal^2 * (1 + (k - 1) * rho) / k
effective_sd <- sqrt(effective_var)

cat("Repeated-Measures ANOVA Analysis\n")
cat("==================================\n")
cat(sprintf("Group 1 mean (μ₁): %.2f\n", mu1))
cat(sprintf("Group 2 mean (μ₂): %.2f\n", mu2))
cat(sprintf("Effect size (Δ = μ₁ - μ₂): %.2f\n", delta))
cat(sprintf("\nMarginal SD at each occasion: %.2f\n", sigma_marginal))
cat(sprintf("Number of repeated measurements: %d\n", k))
cat(sprintf("Compound symmetry correlation (ρ): %.2f\n", rho))
cat(sprintf("\nEffective variance of subject-level average:\n"))
cat(sprintf("  Var(Y̅ᵢ) = σ²(1 + (k-1)ρ)/k = %.4f² × (1 + %d × %.2f) / %d\n", 
            sigma_marginal, k-1, rho, k))
cat(sprintf("         = %.4f × %.2f / %d\n", sigma_marginal^2, 1 + (k-1)*rho, k))
cat(sprintf("         = %.4f\n", effective_var))
cat(sprintf("Effective SD of subject-level average: %.4f\n\n", effective_sd))

# For a two-sample t-test on subject averages:
# The test statistic is t = (Ȳ₁ - Ȳ₂) / SE where
# SE = effective_sd × sqrt(2/n) for equal group sizes n
# 
# This is equivalent to testing the between-group effect in repeated-measures ANOVA
# using subject-level averages

# Critical value for two-sided test with df ≈ 2n - 2
t_crit_approx <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df = 100)  # approximate for larger n
cat(sprintf("Two-sided critical value (two-tailed, α=%.3f): ±%.4f\n\n", alpha, t_crit_approx))

# Function to calculate power for a given sample size per group
calculate_power <- function(n_per_group) {
  df <- 2 * n_per_group - 2
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df = df)
  se <- effective_sd * sqrt(2 / n_per_group)
  ncp <- delta / se  # Non-centrality parameter
  power <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df, ncp) + pt(-t_crit, df, ncp)
  return(power)
}

# Search for minimum sample size achieving target power
# Start with a reasonable guess
n_candidates <- seq(5, 100, by = 1)
powers <- sapply(n_candidates, calculate_power)

# Find the minimum n where power >= 0.80
minimum_n <- min(n_candidates[powers >= target_power])
power_at_min <- calculate_power(minimum_n)
power_at_prev <- calculate_power(minimum_n - 1)

cat("Sample Size Search Results:\n")
cat("============================\n")
cat(sprintf("Minimum participants per group: %d\n", minimum_n))
cat(sprintf("Achieved power at n=%d: %.6f\n", minimum_n, power_at_min))
cat(sprintf("Power at preceding design (n=%d): %.6f\n\n", minimum_n - 1, power_at_prev))

# Display a range of results for verification
cat("Power Analysis Table:\n")
cat("n\tPower\n")
for (n in seq(minimum_n - 3, minimum_n + 2)) {
  if (n > 0) {
    p <- calculate_power(n)
    cat(sprintf("%d\t%.6f\n", n, p))
  }
}

# Store final results for POWER_AGENT_RESULT
result_n <- minimum_n
result_power <- power_at_min

cat("\n\nFinal Result:\n")
cat(sprintf("Minimum sample size: %d participants per group\n", result_n))
cat(sprintf("Achieved power: %.6f\n", result_power))

# Linear regression power calculation: Test R² = 0
# Parameters
n <- 80                      # sample size (participants)
k <- 3                       # number of predictors
rho <- 0.30                  # anticipated multiple correlation
alpha <- 0.05                # significance level (one-sided, upper tail)

# Compute R² from multiple correlation
R_squared <- rho^2
cat("R² (anticipated):", R_squared, "\n")

# Degrees of freedom
df_num <- k                           # numerator df = number of predictors
df_denom <- n - k - 1                # denominator df = n - k - 1
cat("Degrees of freedom: numerator =", df_num, ", denominator =", df_denom, "\n")

# Noncentrality parameter λ
# λ = F_stat × df_denom
# where F_stat = [R²/(1 - R²)] × (df_denom / df_num)
F_stat <- (R_squared / (1 - R_squared)) * (df_denom / df_num)
lambda <- F_stat * df_denom
cat("F-statistic (under H1):", F_stat, "\n")
cat("Noncentrality parameter λ:", lambda, "\n")

# Critical value from central F distribution at α = 0.05 (upper tail)
F_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df1 = df_num, df2 = df_denom)
cat("Critical F-value (α =", alpha, "):", F_crit, "\n")

# Power: P(F > F_crit | H1)
# Under H1, F follows a noncentral F distribution with noncentrality parameter λ
power <- 1 - pf(F_crit, df1 = df_num, df2 = df_denom, ncp = lambda)
cat("\nPower:", power, "\n")

# Summary
cat("\n=== Summary ===\n")
cat("Sample size:", n, "participants\n")
cat("Number of predictors:", k, "\n")
cat("Multiple correlation (ρ):", rho, "\n")
cat("R² (H1):", R_squared, "\n")
cat("Hypothesis: H0: R² = 0 vs H1: R² > 0 (one-sided, upper tail)\n")
cat("Significance level (α):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Power:", round(power, 6), "\n")

# Return result in required format
results <- list(
  metric = "power",
  value = power,
  unit = "probability"
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=", jsonlite::toJSON(list(results = list(results)), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15), "\n", sep = "")

# Independent verification of power for testing R² = 0 in linear regression
# Using a separate implementation to check the candidate's result

# Parameters from the original request
n <- 80                          # sample size
k <- 3                           # number of predictors (excluding intercept)
rho <- 0.30                      # anticipated multiple correlation
alpha <- 0.05                    # significance level (one-sided, upper tail)

# Compute R²
R_sq <- rho^2
cat("Input parameters:\n")
cat("  n =", n, "participants\n")
cat("  k =", k, "predictors\n")
cat("  ρ (multiple correlation) =", rho, "\n")
cat("  R² =", R_sq, "\n")
cat("  α =", alpha, "(one-sided, upper tail)\n\n")

# Degrees of freedom
df1 <- k                        # numerator degrees of freedom
df2 <- n - k - 1                # denominator degrees of freedom
cat("Degrees of freedom:\n")
cat("  df₁ (numerator) =", df1, "\n")
cat("  df₂ (denominator) = n - k - 1 =", n, "-", k, "- 1 =", df2, "\n\n")

# Critical value from the central F distribution (H₀ distribution)
F_crit <- qf(p = 1 - alpha, df1 = df1, df2 = df2, lower.tail = TRUE)
cat("Critical F-value from F(df₁=", df1, ", df₂=", df2, "):\n")
cat("  F_crit = F_{1-α}(", df1, ",", df2, ") = F_{0.95}(", df1, ",", df2, ") =", F_crit, "\n\n")

# Noncentrality parameter
# Under H1, the noncentrality parameter is λ = n × R² / (1 - R²)
# This is the standard parameterization in R's noncentral F functions
lambda <- n * R_sq / (1 - R_sq)
cat("Noncentrality parameter (H1):\n")
cat("  λ = n × R² / (1 - R²)\n")
cat("    = ", n, "×", R_sq, "/", (1 - R_sq), "\n")
cat("    =", lambda, "\n\n")

# Power: P(F > F_crit | H1) using the noncentral F distribution
power <- 1 - pf(q = F_crit, df1 = df1, df2 = df2, ncp = lambda, lower.tail = TRUE)
cat("Power calculation:\n")
cat("  Power = P(F > F_crit | H1)\n")
cat("        = 1 - P(F ≤ F_crit | F ~ F(", df1, ",", df2, "; λ=", lambda, "))\n")
cat("        = 1 - pf(", F_crit, "; df1=", df1, ", df2=", df2, ", ncp=", lambda, ")\n")
cat("        =", power, "\n\n")

# Verify the calculation using an alternative formulation
# F-statistic under H1: F = [R²/(1-R²)] × (df₂/df₁)
F_stat_under_H1 <- (R_sq / (1 - R_sq)) * (df2 / df1)
cat("Verification using F-statistic formula:\n")
cat("  F(under H1) = [R²/(1-R²)] × (df₂/df₁)\n")
cat("              = [", R_sq, "/ ", (1 - R_sq), "] × (", df2, "/", df1, ")\n")
cat("              =", F_stat_under_H1, "\n")
cat("  This F-stat is < F_crit (", F_crit, "), so power should be < 100%\n\n")

# Summary output
cat("=== INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION SUMMARY ===\n")
cat("Study Design: Linear regression testing H₀: R² = 0\n")
cat("Sample size: ", n, "participants\n")
cat("Predictors: ", k, "(plus intercept)\n")
cat("Effect size: ρ = ", rho, "(R² = ", R_sq, ")\n")
cat("Significance level: α = ", alpha, "\n")
cat("Hypothesis: One-sided upper-tail test\n")
cat("Test: Noncentral F(", df1, ",", df2, "; λ=", lambda, ")\n")
cat("Power: ", round(power, 15), "\n")

# Output in required format
results <- list(
  metric = "power",
  value = power,
  unit = "probability"
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=", jsonlite::toJSON(list(results = list(results)), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15), "\n", sep = "")

# Detailed derivation and reference check of noncentrality parameter
# for F-test of H0: R² = 0 in linear regression

cat("=== Noncentrality Parameter Derivation ===\n\n")

# The global F-test for R² = 0 in linear regression is:
# F = (R² / (1 - R²)) * ((n - k - 1) / k) ~ F(k, n-k-1) under H0
# Under H1 (true R² ≠ 0), this follows a noncentral F distribution

# The noncentrality parameter λ for a noncentral F distribution is defined such that:
# If X ~ F(df1, df2; λ), then E[X] = (df2 / (df2 - 2)) * (1 + λ / df1)
# for df2 > 2

# For the R² test specifically:
# Under H1 with true R² = ρ², the noncentrality parameter is:
# λ = n * ρ² / (1 - ρ²)

# This can be verified from the expectation of the test statistic:
# E[F | H1] = (ρ² / (1 - ρ²)) * ((n - k - 1) / k)

# And the relationship: E[F(df1, df2; λ)] = (df2/(df2-2)) * (1 + λ/df1)
# So: (ρ² / (1 - ρ²)) * ((n - k - 1) / k) = (df2/(df2-2)) * (1 + λ/df1)
#
# Solving for λ (approximately for moderate df2):
# λ ≈ df1 * [(ρ² / (1 - ρ²)) * ((n - k - 1) / k) - (df2/(df2-2))]
# But more directly: λ = n * ρ² / (1 - ρ²)

n <- 80
k <- 3
rho <- 0.30
R_sq <- rho^2
alpha <- 0.05

df1 <- k
df2 <- n - k - 1

# Correct λ formula
lambda <- n * R_sq / (1 - R_sq)

cat("Given: n =", n, ", k =", k, ", ρ =", rho, ", R² =", R_sq, "\n\n")

cat("Noncentrality parameter λ:\n")
cat("  λ = n * R² / (1 - R²)\n")
cat("  λ =", n, "*", R_sq, "/", (1 - R_sq), "\n")
cat("  λ =", lambda, "\n\n")

# Verify the expected F-statistic under H1
F_expected_H1 <- (R_sq / (1 - R_sq)) * ((n - k - 1) / k)
cat("Expected F-statistic under H1:\n")
cat("  E[F | H1] = (R² / (1 - R²)) * ((n - k - 1) / k)\n")
cat("  E[F | H1] =", F_expected_H1, "\n\n")

# Verify using the relationship E[F(df1, df2; λ)] = (df2/(df2-2)) * (1 + λ/df1)
E_noncentral_F <- (df2 / (df2 - 2)) * (1 + lambda / df1)
cat("Expected value from noncentral F distribution formula:\n")
cat("  E[F(", df1, ",", df2, ";", lambda, ")] = (", df2, "/(", df2, "-2)) * (1 + ", lambda, "/", df1, ")\n")
cat("  E[F] =", E_noncentral_F, "\n\n")

cat("Comparison:\n")
cat("  F_expected from H1 formula:       ", F_expected_H1, "\n")
cat("  E[F] from noncentral F formula:   ", E_noncentral_F, "\n")
cat("  Difference:                        ", abs(F_expected_H1 - E_noncentral_F), "\n")
cat("  (Small difference due to finite-sample adjustment; λ formula is correct)\n\n")

# Now compute power
F_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df1, df2)
power <- 1 - pf(F_crit, df1, df2, ncp = lambda)

cat("=== Power Calculation ===\n")
cat("Critical F-value at α = 0.05: F_crit =", F_crit, "\n")
cat("Noncentrality parameter: λ =", lambda, "\n")
cat("Power = P(F(", df1, ",", df2, ";", lambda, ") > ", F_crit, ")\n", sep = "")
cat("Power =", power, "\n\n")

# Output in required format
results <- list(
  metric = "power",
  value = power,
  unit = "probability"
)

df_denom <- n - k - 1                # denominator df = n - k - 1

# λ = F_stat × df_denom

# Under H1, F follows a noncentral F distribution with noncentrality parameter λ

library(jsonlite)

# Parameters
n <- 80                      # sample size (participants)
k <- 3                       # number of predictors
rho <- 0.30                  # anticipated multiple correlation
alpha <- 0.05                # significance level (one-sided, upper tail)

# Compute R² from multiple correlation
R_squared <- rho^2
cat("=== Linear Regression Power Calculation ===\n\n")
cat("Given parameters:\n")
cat("  Sample size (n):", n, "participants\n")
cat("  Number of predictors (k):", k, "\n")
cat("  Multiple correlation (ρ):", rho, "\n")
cat("  R² = ρ²:", R_squared, "\n")
cat("  Significance level (α):", alpha, "(one-sided, upper tail)\n\n")

# Degrees of freedom
df_num <- k
df_denom <- n - k - 1
cat("Degrees of freedom:\n")
cat("  Numerator (df₁):", df_num, "\n")
cat("  Denominator (df₂):", df_denom, "\n\n")

# Critical F value from central F(df1, df2) distribution
F_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df1 = df_num, df2 = df_denom)
cat("Critical value:\n")
cat("  F_crit = F₀.₉₅(3, 76) =", F_crit, "\n\n")

# CORRECT noncentrality parameter formula
# λ = n × R² / (1 - R²)
lambda_correct <- n * R_squared / (1 - R_squared)
cat("Noncentrality parameter (CORRECT FORMULA):\n")
cat("  λ = n × R² / (1 - R²)\n")
cat("  λ = 80 × 0.09 / 0.91\n")
cat("  λ =", lambda_correct, "\n\n")

# Compute power using noncentral F distribution
power <- 1 - pf(F_crit, df1 = df_num, df2 = df_denom, ncp = lambda_correct)
cat("Power calculation:\n")
cat("  Power = P(F > F_crit | H₁)\n")
cat("  Power = P(F(3, 76; λ = 7.912) > 2.725)\n")
cat("  Power =", power, "\n\n")

# Identification of error in first execution
cat("=== Error Identification ===\n")
cat("Evidence e1 used INCORRECT formula:\n")
cat("  F_stat = (R² / (1 - R²)) × (df_denom / df_num) = 2.505495\n")
cat("  λ_WRONG = F_stat × df_denom = 2.505495 × 76 = 190.4176\n")
cat("  This produced power ≈ 1.0 (incorrect)\n\n")
cat("Evidence e2 uses CORRECT formula:\n")
cat("  λ_CORRECT = n × R² / (1 - R²) = 80 × 0.09 / 0.91 = 7.912088\n")
cat("  This produces power = 0.6238 (correct)\n\n")

# Final result
cat("=== FINAL RESULT ===\n")
cat("Power:", round(power, 15), "\n")

# Return result in required format
results <- list(
  metric = "power",
  value = power,
  unit = "probability"
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=", toJSON(list(results = list(results)), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15), "\n", sep = "")

alpha <- 0.05        # significance level

# Derived quantities

df1 <- k             # numerator df = number of predictors
df2 <- n - k - 1     # denominator df = n - k - 1

cat("=== Independent Verification ===\n")
cat("Parameters:\n")
cat("  n =", n, ", k =", k, ", ρ =", rho, ", α =", alpha, "\n")
cat("  R² =", R_sq, "\n")
cat("  df1 =", df1, ", df2 =", df2, "\n\n")

F_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df1, df2)
cat("Critical F-value (upper 0.05 tail of F(3,76)):\n")
cat("  F_crit =", F_crit, "\n\n")

# Correct noncentrality parameter formula
# The noncentrality parameter for the F-test of global R² is:
# λ = n * R² / (1 - R²)
# This comes from the fact that the test statistic under H1 is:
# F = [R²/(1-R²)] * [(n-k-1)/k] ~ F(k, n-k-1; λ)
# where λ = n * R² / (1 - R²)

lambda <- n * R_sq / (1 - R_sq)
cat("Noncentrality parameter (correct formula):\n")
cat("  λ = n * R² / (1 - R²)\n")
cat("  λ =", n, "*", R_sq, "/", (1 - R_sq), "\n")
cat("  λ =", lambda, "\n\n")

# Power: probability of rejecting H0 given H1 is true
# Power = P(F > F_crit | H1) = P(F(df1, df2; λ) > F_crit)
power <- 1 - pf(F_crit, df1, df2, ncp = lambda)
cat("Power calculation:\n")
cat("  Power = 1 - pf(F_crit=", F_crit, ", df1=", df1, ", df2=", df2, ", ncp=", lambda, ")\n")
cat("  Power =", power, "\n\n")

# Detailed derivation and reference check of noncentrality parameter
# for F-test of H0: R² = 0 in linear regression

cat("=== Noncentrality Parameter Derivation ===\n\n")

# The global F-test for R² = 0 in linear regression is:
# F = (R² / (1 - R²)) * ((n - k - 1) / k) ~ F(k, n-k-1) under H0
# Under H1 (true R² ≠ 0), this follows a noncentral F distribution

# The noncentrality parameter λ for a noncentral F distribution is defined such that:
# If X ~ F(df1, df2; λ), then E[X] = (df2 / (df2 - 2)) * (1 + λ / df1)
# for df2 > 2

# For the R² test specifically:
# Under H1 with true R² = ρ², the noncentrality parameter is:
# λ = n * ρ² / (1 - ρ²)

# This can be verified from the expectation of the test statistic:
# E[F | H1] = (ρ² / (1 - ρ²)) * ((n - k - 1) / k)

# And the relationship: E[F(df1, df2; λ)] = (df2/(df2-2)) * (1 + λ/df1)
# So: (ρ² / (1 - ρ²)) * ((n - k - 1) / k) = (df2/(df2-2)) * (1 + λ/df1)
#
# Solving for λ (approximately for moderate df2):
# λ ≈ df1 * [(ρ² / (1 - ρ²)) * ((n - k - 1) / k) - (df2/(df2-2))]
# But more directly: λ = n * ρ² / (1 - ρ²)

n <- 80
k <- 3
rho <- 0.30
R_sq <- rho^2
alpha <- 0.05

df1 <- k
df2 <- n - k - 1

# Correct λ formula
lambda <- n * R_sq / (1 - R_sq)

cat("Given: n =", n, ", k =", k, ", ρ =", rho, ", R² =", R_sq, "\n\n")

cat("Noncentrality parameter λ:\n")
cat("  λ = n * R² / (1 - R²)\n")
cat("  λ =", n, "*", R_sq, "/", (1 - R_sq), "\n")
cat("  λ =", lambda, "\n\n")

# Verify the expected F-statistic under H1
F_expected_H1 <- (R_sq / (1 - R_sq)) * ((n - k - 1) / k)
cat("Expected F-statistic under H1:\n")
cat("  E[F | H1] = (R² / (1 - R²)) * ((n - k - 1) / k)\n")
cat("  E[F | H1] =", F_expected_H1, "\n\n")

# Verify using the relationship E[F(df1, df2; λ)] = (df2/(df2-2)) * (1 + λ/df1)
E_noncentral_F <- (df2 / (df2 - 2)) * (1 + lambda / df1)
cat("Expected value from noncentral F distribution formula:\n")
cat("  E[F(", df1, ",", df2, ";", lambda, ")] = (", df2, "/(", df2, "-2)) * (1 + ", lambda, "/", df1, ")\n")
cat("  E[F] =", E_noncentral_F, "\n\n")

cat("Comparison:\n")
cat("  F_expected from H1 formula:       ", F_expected_H1, "\n")
cat("  E[F] from noncentral F formula:   ", E_noncentral_F, "\n")

cat("=== Power Calculation ===\n")
cat("Critical F-value at α = 0.05: F_crit =", F_crit, "\n")
cat("Noncentrality parameter: λ =", lambda, "\n")
cat("Power = P(F(", df1, ",", df2, ";", lambda, ") > ", F_crit, ")\n", sep = "")

library(jsonlite)

# Design parameters
n_per_group <- 32
difference <- 4.3  # Expected difference in means (dBA)
common_sd <- 7.8   # Common standard deviation (dBA)
alpha <- 0.05      # Significance level
df <- 2 * n_per_group - 2  # Degrees of freedom

# Cohen's d effect size
cohens_d <- difference / common_sd

# Non-centrality parameter
# For two independent samples with equal n: 
# lambda = (mu1 - mu2) / (sd * sqrt(2/n)) = d * sqrt(n/2)
lambda <- cohens_d * sqrt(n_per_group / 2)

# Critical value for one-sided test at alpha = 0.05
# H_A: mu1 > mu2, so upper tail
t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df)

# Power = P(T > t_crit | H_A true) under non-central t distribution
power <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df, ncp = lambda)

# Round to reasonable precision
power_rounded <- round(power, 4)

# Summary
cat("Two-Sample t-Test Power Calculation\n")
cat("=====================================\n")
cat(sprintf("Sample size per group: %d\n", n_per_group))
cat(sprintf("Total sample size: %d\n", 2 * n_per_group))
cat(sprintf("Expected difference: %.1f dBA\n", difference))
cat(sprintf("Common standard deviation: %.1f dBA\n", common_sd))
cat(sprintf("Cohen's d effect size: %.4f\n", cohens_d))
cat(sprintf("Degrees of freedom: %d\n", df))
cat(sprintf("Significance level (alpha): %.4f (one-sided, upper tail)\n", alpha))
cat(sprintf("Critical t-value: %.4f\n", t_crit))
cat(sprintf("Non-centrality parameter (lambda): %.4f\n", lambda))
cat(sprintf("Power: %.4f\n", power_rounded))

# Output for structured reporting
results <- data.frame(
  metric = "power",
  value = power_rounded,
  unit = "probability"
)

cat("\n\nStructured Output:\n")
cat(toJSON(list(results = results), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

library(jsonlite)

# Design parameters
n_per_group <- 32
difference <- 4.3  # Expected difference in means (dBA)
common_sd <- 7.8   # Common standard deviation (dBA)
alpha <- 0.05      # Significance level
df <- 2 * n_per_group - 2  # Degrees of freedom

# Cohen's d effect size
cohens_d <- difference / common_sd

# Non-centrality parameter
# For two independent samples with equal n: 
# lambda = (mu1 - mu2) / (sd * sqrt(2/n)) = d * sqrt(n/2)
lambda <- cohens_d * sqrt(n_per_group / 2)

# Critical value for one-sided test at alpha = 0.05
# H_A: mu1 > mu2, so upper tail
t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df)

# Power = P(T > t_crit | H_A true) under non-central t distribution
power <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df, ncp = lambda)

# Round to reasonable precision
power_rounded <- round(power, 4)

# Summary
cat("Two-Sample t-Test Power Calculation\n")
cat("=====================================\n")
cat(sprintf("Sample size per group: %d\n", n_per_group))
cat(sprintf("Total sample size: %d\n", 2 * n_per_group))
cat(sprintf("Expected difference: %.1f dBA\n", difference))
cat(sprintf("Common standard deviation: %.1f dBA\n", common_sd))
cat(sprintf("Cohen's d effect size: %.4f\n", cohens_d))
cat(sprintf("Degrees of freedom: %d\n", df))
cat(sprintf("Significance level (alpha): %.4f (one-sided, upper tail)\n", alpha))
cat(sprintf("Critical t-value: %.4f\n", t_crit))
cat(sprintf("Non-centrality parameter (lambda): %.4f\n", lambda))
cat(sprintf("Power: %.4f\n", power_rounded))

# Output for structured reporting
results <- data.frame(
  metric = "power",
  value = power_rounded,
  unit = "probability"
)

cat("\n\nStructured Output:\n")
cat(toJSON(list(results = results), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

# Evidence e1; success=true

library(jsonlite)

# Design parameters
n_per_group <- 32
difference <- 4.3  # Expected difference in means (dBA)
common_sd <- 7.8   # Common standard deviation (dBA)
alpha <- 0.05      # Significance level
df <- 2 * n_per_group - 2  # Degrees of freedom

# Cohen's d effect size
cohens_d <- difference / common_sd

# Non-centrality parameter
# For two independent samples with equal n: 
# lambda = (mu1 - mu2) / (sd * sqrt(2/n)) = d * sqrt(n/2)
lambda <- cohens_d * sqrt(n_per_group / 2)

# Critical value for one-sided test at alpha = 0.05
# H_A: mu1 > mu2, so upper tail
t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df)

# Power = P(T > t_crit | H_A true) under non-central t distribution
power <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df, ncp = lambda)

# Round to reasonable precision
power_rounded <- round(power, 4)

# Summary
cat("Two-Sample t-Test Power Calculation\n")
cat("=====================================\n")
cat(sprintf("Sample size per group: %d\n", n_per_group))
cat(sprintf("Total sample size: %d\n", 2 * n_per_group))
cat(sprintf("Expected difference: %.1f dBA\n", difference))
cat(sprintf("Common standard deviation: %.1f dBA\n", common_sd))
cat(sprintf("Cohen's d effect size: %.4f\n", cohens_d))
cat(sprintf("Degrees of freedom: %d\n", df))
cat(sprintf("Significance level (alpha): %.4f (one-sided, upper tail)\n", alpha))
cat(sprintf("Critical t-value: %.4f\n", t_crit))
cat(sprintf("Non-centrality parameter (lambda): %.4f\n", lambda))
cat(sprintf("Power: %.4f\n", power_rounded))

# Output for structured reporting
results <- data.frame(
  metric = "power",
  value = power_rounded,
  unit = "probability"
)

cat("\n\nStructured Output:\n")
cat(toJSON(list(results = results), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

  # Generate samples
  group1 <- rnorm(n_per_group, mean = 0, sd = common_sd)

  # Perform pooled t-test (one-sided, upper tail: H_A: mu1 > mu2)

# Two-sample t-test power calculation
# Study design: independent normal means with equal variances
# Hypothesis: one-sided test of superiority

# Parameters from user specification
effect_size_raw <- 4.3    # Expected difference (dBA)
common_sd <- 7.8          # Common standard deviation (dBA)
n_per_group <- 32         # Sample size per group
alpha <- 0.05             # Significance level
sidedness <- 1            # One-sided test
df_error <- 2 * n_per_group - 2  # Degrees of freedom

# Calculate Cohen's d (standardized effect size)
cohens_d <- effect_size_raw / common_sd

# Calculate noncentrality parameter λ
# For equal sample sizes: λ = (μ1 - μ2) / σ * sqrt(n/2)
# Which equals: effect_size / σ * sqrt(n1 * n2 / (n1 + n2))
lambda <- (effect_size_raw / common_sd) * sqrt((n_per_group * n_per_group) / (n_per_group + n_per_group))

# Equivalently for equal n:
lambda_check <- cohens_d * sqrt(n_per_group / 2)

# Critical value for one-sided test at alpha 0.05
t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df = df_error, ncp = 0)

# Power = P(t > t_crit | H1 true) where t follows noncentral t distribution
power <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df = df_error, ncp = lambda)

# Output results
cat("Two-Sample Pooled t-Test Power Calculation\n")
cat("===========================================\n")
cat("Study Design Parameters:\n")
cat("  Expected difference in means:", effect_size_raw, "dBA\n")
cat("  Common standard deviation:", common_sd, "dBA\n")
cat("  Sample size per group:", n_per_group, "\n")
cat("  Total sample size:", 2 * n_per_group, "\n")
cat("  Significance level (alpha):", alpha, "\n")
cat("  Sidedness: one-sided\n")
cat("  Degrees of freedom:", df_error, "\n")
cat("\nEffect Size:\n")
cat("  Cohen's d:", round(cohens_d, 6), "\n")
cat("  Noncentrality parameter λ:", round(lambda, 6), "\n")
cat("  Noncentrality check λ:", round(lambda_check, 6), "\n")
cat("\nTest Specification:\n")
cat("  Critical value (t_crit):", round(t_crit, 6), "\n")
cat("  One-sided test: H0: μ1 ≤ μ2 vs H1: μ1 > μ2\n")
cat("\nResults:\n")
cat("  Power:", round(power, 6), "\n")

# Format result for submission
result_power <- power
result_metric <- "power"
result_unit <- "probability"

jsonlite::toJSON(
  list(
    results = list(
      list(metric = result_metric, value = result_power, unit = result_unit)
    )
  ),
  auto_unbox = TRUE,
  digits = 15
)

answer.summary: Using pmsampsize 1.1.3 Riley binary prediction model development criteria with 10 candidate predictor parameters, outcome prevalence of 0.20, anticipated Cox-Snell R-squared of 0.12, and shrinkage factor of 0.95, the minimum total sample size required is 1482 participants. This sample size is driven by Criterion 1 (overfitting control with shrinkage of 0.95), which requires the largest sample. The achieved margin of error for predicted outcome risk at this sample size is 0.020365 (95% CI: [0.179635, 0.220365]), which is well below the target of 0.05, satisfying the precision criterion for outcome-risk estimation.
answer.method: Riley (2018, 2020) binary prediction model sample size calculation implemented in pmsampsize 1.1.3. The method evaluates three criteria: (1) overfitting control via shrinkage of predictor effects to ≥0.95; (2) precision of R-squared estimation with absolute difference ≤0.05 (Nagelkerke scale); (3) precise estimation of average outcome risk within ±0.05 at 95% confidence. The recommended sample size is the maximum required across all three criteria.
assumptions: Binary outcome prediction model development

Anticipated Cox-Snell R-squared is 0.12

limitations: No adjustment for missing data or subject attrition applied; specification would require additional analysis
Sample size does not account for potential data quality issues or variable selection changes during development
Assumes outcome prevalence of 0.20 is accurate; sensitivity analysis recommended for alternative prevalence values

# Install and load pmsampsize package
if (!require("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize", repos = "https://cran.r-project.org")
  library("pmsampsize")
}

# Check package version
packageVersion("pmsampsize")

# Calculate sample size using Riley binary criteria
# Parameters:
# - type: "binary" for binary outcome prediction model
# - params: list of parameters
#   * pmvd: average outcome-risk margin of error (0.05)
#   * prev: prevalence of outcome (0.20)
#   * rsq: Cox-Snell R-squared (0.12)
#   * shrinkage: intercept shrinkage (0.95)
#   * pd: apparent R-squared difference (0.05, default for absolute precision)
#   * ndf: number of candidate predictors (10)

result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "binary",
  params = list(
    pmvd = 0.05,           # absolute margin of error for outcome risk
    prev = 0.20,           # outcome prevalence
    rsq = 0.12,            # Cox-Snell R-squared
    shrinkage = 0.95,      # shrinkage factor
    ndf = 10               # number of candidate predictors
  )
)

# Display results
cat("=== pmsampsize Riley Binary Development Results ===\n\n")
print(result)

# Extract sample size
sample_size <- result$N

cat("\n\n=== EXTRACTED VALUES ===\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size required:", sample_size, "participants\n")
cat("Method: Riley binary prediction model development criteria\n")
cat("Outcome prevalence:", 0.20, "\n")
cat("Cox-Snell R-squared (anticipated):", 0.12, "\n")
cat("Shrinkage factor:", 0.95, "\n")
cat("Outcome risk margin of error (absolute):", 0.05, "\n")
cat("Number of candidate predictors:", 10, "\n")
cat("Confidence level:", 0.95, "\n")
cat("Maximum absolute R-squared difference (Nagelkerke):", 0.05, "\n")

# Verify precision at returned sample size
# At the calculated sample size, verify that the precision criterion is met
# For binary outcome: margin of error for estimated outcome risk should be ≤ 0.05

# Approximate verification:
# Standard error of predicted outcome risk ≈ sqrt(p(1-p)/n)
# At 95% confidence: margin of error ≈ 1.96 * SE
p <- 0.20
n <- sample_size
se_predicted_risk <- sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
me_predicted_risk <- 1.96 * se_predicted_risk

cat("\n=== PRECISION VERIFICATION AT RETURNED SAMPLE SIZE ===\n")
cat("Outcome prevalence (p):", p, "\n")
cat("Sample size (n):", n, "\n")
cat("Standard error of predicted risk:", round(se_predicted_risk, 6), "\n")
cat("Margin of error at 95% confidence:", round(me_predicted_risk, 6), "\n")
cat("Target margin of error:", 0.05, "\n")
cat("Precision criterion met?", "ME =", round(me_predicted_risk, 6), "≤ 0.05:", 
    me_predicted_risk <= 0.05, "\n")

# Return result
cat("\n\n=== FINAL RESULT ===\n")
cat("SAMPLE_SIZE=", sample_size, " participants\n")

# JSON output for POWER_AGENT_RESULT
library(jsonlite)
results_json <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = sample_size, unit = "participants_total"),
    list(metric = "outcome_prevalence", value = 0.20, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "cox_snell_rsquared", value = 0.12, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "shrinkage_factor", value = 0.95, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "margin_of_error_achieved", value = round(me_predicted_risk, 6), unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "candidate_predictors", value = 10, unit = "count"),
    list(metric = "number_of_events_expected", value = round(n * p), unit = "count")
  )
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=", toJSON(results_json, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15), "\n")

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,
       rsquared = NA,
       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,
       prevalence = NA,
       cstatistic = NA,
       seed = 123456,
       rate = NA,
       timepoint = NA,
       meanfup = NA,
       intercept = NA,
       sd = NA,
       mmoe = 1.1
     )
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

     A list including a matrix of calculated sample size requirements
     for each criteria defined under _'Details'_, and a series of
     vectors of parameters used in the calculations as well as the
     final recommended minimum sample size and number of events
     required for model development.

     Collins GS. Minimum sample size required for developing a

_ E_ x_ a_ m_ p_ l_ e_ s:

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

# Load pmsampsize
library("pmsampsize")
library("jsonlite")

# Calculate sample size using Riley binary criteria
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "b",
  csrsquared = 0.12,      # Cox-Snell R-squared
  parameters = 10,         # number of candidate predictors
  prevalence = 0.20,       # outcome prevalence
  shrinkage = 0.95         # shrinkage factor
)

# Extract values from result object
min_sample_size <- result$sample_size
min_events <- result$events
prevalence <- result$prevalence
cox_snell <- result$rsquared
final_shrinkage <- result$final_shrinkage
parameters <- result$parameters
nagelkerke_rsq <- result$nag_r2
epp <- result$EPP

cat("=== pmsampsize Riley Binary Development Results ===\n\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size required:", min_sample_size, "participants\n")
cat("Minimum number of events required:", min_events, "events\n")
cat("Final shrinkage achieved:", final_shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Parameters:", parameters, "\n")
cat("Cox-Snell R-squared:", cox_snell, "\n")
cat("Nagelkerke R-squared:", nagelkerke_rsq, "\n")
cat("Events per predictor (EPP):", epp, "\n")
cat("Outcome prevalence:", prevalence, "\n")

# Verify precision at returned sample size for outcome risk estimation
# The third criterion in Riley binary is: precise estimation (within ±0.05) of average outcome risk
# at 95% confidence level

# Standard error of predicted outcome risk ≈ sqrt(p(1-p)/n)
# At 95% confidence: margin of error ≈ 1.96 * SE
p <- prevalence
n <- min_sample_size
se_predicted_risk <- sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
me_predicted_risk <- 1.96 * se_predicted_risk

cat("\n=== PRECISION VERIFICATION AT RETURNED SAMPLE SIZE ===\n")
cat("Outcome prevalence (p):", p, "\n")
cat("Sample size (n):", n, "\n")
cat("Standard error of predicted risk:", format(se_predicted_risk, digits = 6), "\n")
cat("Margin of error at 95% confidence:", format(me_predicted_risk, digits = 6), "\n")
cat("Target margin of error:", 0.05, "\n")
cat("Precision criterion met (ME ≤ 0.05)?:", me_predicted_risk <= 0.05, "\n")

# Calculate 95% CI for predicted outcome risk
ci_lower <- p - me_predicted_risk
ci_upper <- p + me_predicted_risk

cat("\n95% Confidence Interval for predicted outcome risk:\n")
cat("Point estimate (prevalence):", p, "\n")
cat("95% CI: [", format(ci_lower, digits = 4), ",", format(ci_upper, digits = 4), "]\n")
cat("CI width (total margin):", format(2 * me_predicted_risk, digits = 6), "\n")

# Return result
cat("\n\n=== FINAL RESULT FOR STRUCTURED REPORTING ===\n")
cat("Primary metric: sample_size\n")
cat("Value:", min_sample_size, "\n")
cat("Unit: participants_total\n")

# JSON output for POWER_AGENT_RESULT
results_json <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = min_sample_size, unit = "participants_total"),
    list(metric = "minimum_number_of_events", value = min_events, unit = "events"),
    list(metric = "outcome_prevalence", value = prevalence, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "cox_snell_rsquared", value = cox_snell, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "nagelkerke_rsquared", value = nagelkerke_rsq, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "shrinkage_factor", value = final_shrinkage, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "candidate_predictors", value = parameters, unit = "count"),
    list(metric = "events_per_predictor", value = epp, unit = "ratio"),
    list(metric = "margin_of_error_at_sample_size", value = round(me_predicted_risk, 6), unit = "proportion"),

  )
)

# Install and load pmsampsize package
if (!require("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize", repos = "https://cran.r-project.org")
  library("pmsampsize")
}

# Check package version
packageVersion("pmsampsize")

# Calculate sample size using Riley binary criteria
# Parameters:
# - type: "binary" for binary outcome prediction model
# - params: list of parameters
#   * pmvd: average outcome-risk margin of error (0.05)
#   * prev: prevalence of outcome (0.20)
#   * rsq: Cox-Snell R-squared (0.12)
#   * shrinkage: intercept shrinkage (0.95)
#   * pd: apparent R-squared difference (0.05, default for absolute precision)
#   * ndf: number of candidate predictors (10)

result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "binary",
  params = list(
    pmvd = 0.05,           # absolute margin of error for outcome risk
    prev = 0.20,           # outcome prevalence
    rsq = 0.12,            # Cox-Snell R-squared
    shrinkage = 0.95,      # shrinkage factor
    ndf = 10               # number of candidate predictors
  )
)

# Display results
cat("=== pmsampsize Riley Binary Development Results ===\n\n")
print(result)

# Extract sample size
sample_size <- result$N

cat("\n\n=== EXTRACTED VALUES ===\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size required:", sample_size, "participants\n")
cat("Method: Riley binary prediction model development criteria\n")
cat("Outcome prevalence:", 0.20, "\n")
cat("Cox-Snell R-squared (anticipated):", 0.12, "\n")
cat("Shrinkage factor:", 0.95, "\n")
cat("Outcome risk margin of error (absolute):", 0.05, "\n")
cat("Number of candidate predictors:", 10, "\n")
cat("Confidence level:", 0.95, "\n")
cat("Maximum absolute R-squared difference (Nagelkerke):", 0.05, "\n")

# Verify precision at returned sample size
# At the calculated sample size, verify that the precision criterion is met
# For binary outcome: margin of error for estimated outcome risk should be ≤ 0.05

# Approximate verification:
# Standard error of predicted outcome risk ≈ sqrt(p(1-p)/n)
# At 95% confidence: margin of error ≈ 1.96 * SE
p <- 0.20
n <- sample_size
se_predicted_risk <- sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
me_predicted_risk <- 1.96 * se_predicted_risk

cat("\n=== PRECISION VERIFICATION AT RETURNED SAMPLE SIZE ===\n")
cat("Outcome prevalence (p):", p, "\n")
cat("Sample size (n):", n, "\n")
cat("Standard error of predicted risk:", round(se_predicted_risk, 6), "\n")
cat("Margin of error at 95% confidence:", round(me_predicted_risk, 6), "\n")
cat("Target margin of error:", 0.05, "\n")
cat("Precision criterion met?", "ME =", round(me_predicted_risk, 6), "≤ 0.05:", 
    me_predicted_risk <= 0.05, "\n")

# Return result
cat("\n\n=== FINAL RESULT ===\n")
cat("SAMPLE_SIZE=", sample_size, " participants\n")

# JSON output for POWER_AGENT_RESULT
library(jsonlite)
results_json <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = sample_size, unit = "participants_total"),
    list(metric = "outcome_prevalence", value = 0.20, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "cox_snell_rsquared", value = 0.12, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "shrinkage_factor", value = 0.95, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "margin_of_error_achieved", value = round(me_predicted_risk, 6), unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "candidate_predictors", value = 10, unit = "count"),
    list(metric = "number_of_events_expected", value = round(n * p), unit = "count")
  )
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=", toJSON(results_json, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15), "\n")

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

#   * ndf: number of candidate predictors (10)

result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "binary",
  params = list(
    pmvd = 0.05,           # absolute margin of error for outcome risk
    prev = 0.20,           # outcome prevalence
    rsq = 0.12,            # Cox-Snell R-squared
    shrinkage = 0.95,      # shrinkage factor
    ndf = 10               # number of candidate predictors
  )
)

cat("\n\n=== FINAL RESULT ===\n")
cat("SAMPLE_SIZE=", sample_size, " participants\n")

# Load pmsampsize
library("pmsampsize")
library("jsonlite")

# Calculate sample size using Riley binary criteria
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "b",
  csrsquared = 0.12,      # Cox-Snell R-squared
  parameters = 10,         # number of candidate predictors
  prevalence = 0.20,       # outcome prevalence
  shrinkage = 0.95         # shrinkage factor
)

# Extract values from result object
min_sample_size <- result$sample_size
min_events <- result$events
prevalence <- result$prevalence
cox_snell <- result$rsquared
final_shrinkage <- result$final_shrinkage
parameters <- result$parameters
nagelkerke_rsq <- result$nag_r2
epp <- result$EPP

cat("=== pmsampsize Riley Binary Development Results ===\n\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size required:", min_sample_size, "participants\n")
cat("Minimum number of events required:", min_events, "events\n")
cat("Final shrinkage achieved:", final_shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Parameters:", parameters, "\n")
cat("Cox-Snell R-squared:", cox_snell, "\n")
cat("Nagelkerke R-squared:", nagelkerke_rsq, "\n")
cat("Events per predictor (EPP):", epp, "\n")
cat("Outcome prevalence:", prevalence, "\n")

# Verify precision at returned sample size for outcome risk estimation
# The third criterion in Riley binary is: precise estimation (within ±0.05) of average outcome risk
# at 95% confidence level

# Standard error of predicted outcome risk ≈ sqrt(p(1-p)/n)
# At 95% confidence: margin of error ≈ 1.96 * SE
p <- prevalence
n <- min_sample_size
se_predicted_risk <- sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
me_predicted_risk <- 1.96 * se_predicted_risk

cat("\n=== PRECISION VERIFICATION AT RETURNED SAMPLE SIZE ===\n")
cat("Outcome prevalence (p):", p, "\n")
cat("Sample size (n):", n, "\n")
cat("Standard error of predicted risk:", format(se_predicted_risk, digits = 6), "\n")
cat("Margin of error at 95% confidence:", format(me_predicted_risk, digits = 6), "\n")
cat("Target margin of error:", 0.05, "\n")
cat("Precision criterion met (ME ≤ 0.05)?:", me_predicted_risk <= 0.05, "\n")

# Calculate 95% CI for predicted outcome risk
ci_lower <- p - me_predicted_risk
ci_upper <- p + me_predicted_risk

cat("\n95% Confidence Interval for predicted outcome risk:\n")
cat("Point estimate (prevalence):", p, "\n")
cat("95% CI: [", format(ci_lower, digits = 4), ",", format(ci_upper, digits = 4), "]\n")
cat("CI width (total margin):", format(2 * me_predicted_risk, digits = 6), "\n")

# Return result
cat("\n\n=== FINAL RESULT FOR STRUCTURED REPORTING ===\n")
cat("Primary metric: sample_size\n")
cat("Value:", min_sample_size, "\n")
cat("Unit: participants_total\n")

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,
       rsquared = NA,
       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,
       prevalence = NA,
       cstatistic = NA,

       rate = NA,
