     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

answer.summary: Using pmsampsize 1.1.3 with Riley binary prediction model development criteria, the minimum total sample size required is **1,482 participants** (296 events, 1,186 non-events). This sample size meets all three Riley precision criteria: (i) sufficient shrinkage (95% retention of predictor effects), (ii) small discrimination/calibration difference (controlled via shrinkage on Nagelkerke R-squared scale), and (iii) precise average outcome-risk estimation with achieved absolute margin of error of 0.0204 (well below the target 0.05). With 10 candidate predictor parameters and 20% outcome prevalence, the design achieves 29.64 events per parameter, supporting stable model estimation.
answer.method: pmsampsize 1.1.3 binary logistic regression prediction model development with Riley criteria. The method calculates minimum sample size by examining three criteria: (i) overfitting control via shrinkage (target ≥90%), (ii) calibration precision via Nagelkerke R-squared difference (max |apparent - adjusted| ≤0.05), and (iii) outcome-risk precision via 95% confidence interval margin of error (max ±0.05). The returned sample size is the maximum across all three criteria. Outcome-risk precision is verified using the normal approximation: ME = z₍α/₂₎√[p(1-p)/N], where p=0.20 is outcome prevalence and N=1,482 is the returned sample size.
assumptions: Binary logistic regression prediction model with multivariable maximum likelihood estimation
10 candidate predictor parameters included in the final model
Outcome prevalence of 0.20 (20%) expected in the development dataset
Anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared of 0.12 based on previous evidence or conservative expectation
Shrinkage factor of 0.95 representing 5% uniform shrinkage of predictor coefficients to address overfitting
Two-sided 95% confidence level (α=0.05) for outcome-risk margin of error calculation
Default Riley precision criteria: (i) shrinkage ≥90%, (ii) |apparent - adjusted Nagelkerke R²| ≤0.05, (iii) outcome-risk ME ≤0.05
Development cohort without external validation; apparent and adjusted discrimination estimated within the derivation sample using specified shrinkage
limitations: Riley criteria are designed for derivation cohort development and do not include external validation; separate validation cohort recommended to assess genuine model performance
Sample size calculation assumes Cox-Snell R-squared value of 0.12 is accurate; sensitivity analysis with alternative R-squared values recommended if uncertainty exists
Shrinkage factor 0.95 is user-specified; actual overfitting depends on variable selection method and model complexity during development
Outcome-risk precision verification assumes binomial distribution is appropriate; extreme prevalence values may require alternative approaches
The calculation does not account for missing data, loss to follow-up, or withdrawal; additional sample size inflation may be needed if these are anticipated
Events-per-parameter ratio (29.64) is adequate but near-boundary for stable estimation; lower event rates may reduce model stability or increase uncertainty in coefficient estimates

# Parameters from user request:
# - 10 candidate predictors
# - Prevalence: 0.20
# - Anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared: 0.12
# - Shrinkage factor: 0.95
# - Default absolute precision criteria

# Call pmsampsize with binary model development
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "b",           # binary logistic regression
  r2 = 0.12,           # anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
  p = 10,              # number of candidate predictors
  prevalence = 0.20,   # outcome prevalence
  shrinkage = 0.95     # shrinkage factor
  # Using defaults: 
  # precision (overfitting) = 0.05 on Nagelkerke scale
  # outcome.risk.margin = 0.05 for calibration
)

print(result)

# Extract the minimum total sample size
min_sample_size <- ceiling(result$sample_size_based_on_R2)
cat("\n=== RILEY BINARY SAMPLE SIZE CALCULATION ===\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size (based on R-squared precision):", min_sample_size, "\n")
cat("Sample size from object (may be non-integer):", result$sample_size_based_on_R2, "\n")

# Store result for verification
sample_size_integer <- min_sample_size

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,

       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,
       prevalence = NA,
       cstatistic = NA,
       seed = 123456,

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

library(pmsampsize)

# Riley binary development criteria
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "b",              
  csrsquared = 0.12,       
  parameters = 10,         
  prevalence = 0.20,       
  shrinkage = 0.95         
)

# Extract key results
min_sample_size <- result$sample_size
n_events <- result$events
prevalence <- result$prevalence
parameters <- result$parameters
cs_r2 <- result$rsquared
nag_r2 <- result$nag_r2
epp <- result$EPP
final_shrinkage <- result$final_shrinkage

cat("=== RILEY BINARY PREDICTION MODEL DEVELOPMENT ===\n\n")
cat("PRIMARY RESULT:\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size required:", min_sample_size, "participants\n")
cat("Number of events:", n_events, "\n")
cat("Number of non-events:", min_sample_size - n_events, "\n\n")

cat("MODEL SPECIFICATION:\n")
cat("Number of candidate predictor parameters:", parameters, "\n")
cat("Outcome prevalence:", prevalence, "\n")
cat("Anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared:", cs_r2, "\n")
cat("Nagelkerke R-squared (on 0-1 scale):", nag_r2, "\n")
cat("Final shrinkage factor:", final_shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Events per Parameter (EPP):", round(epp, 2), "\n\n")

# Verify outcome-risk precision (Criterion 3)
# For binary models, the margin of error in outcome risk estimation is:
# ME = z_{alpha/2} * sqrt(p(1-p)/n)
# where p is prevalence and n is sample size
# Target margin of error = 0.05 (user-specified)

z_alpha_2 <- qnorm(1 - 0.05/2)  # 95% CI, two-sided
margin_of_error <- z_alpha_2 * sqrt(prevalence * (1 - prevalence) / min_sample_size)

cat("OUTCOME-RISK PRECISION VERIFICATION (Criterion 3):\n")
cat("Z-critical value (95% CI):", round(z_alpha_2, 4), "\n")
cat("Calculated absolute margin of error in average outcome risk:", 
    round(margin_of_error, 4), "\n")
cat("Target margin of error (from user):", 0.05, "\n")
cat("Criterion met (MoE <= 0.05)?:", 
    ifelse(margin_of_error <= 0.05, "YES", "NO"), "\n\n")

# Verify discrimination/calibration precision (Criterion 2)
# The difference between apparent and adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared should be <= 0.05
# This is implicit in the calculation, as pmsampsize uses shrinkage to estimate this

cat("DISCRIMINATION/CALIBRATION PRECISION (Criterion 2):\n")
cat("Difference threshold (Nagelkerke R-squared):", 0.05, "\n")
cat("NB: pmsampsize ensures this via shrinkage factor specification\n\n")

# Results table summary
cat("CRITERIA SUMMARY TABLE:\n")
print(result$results_table)

cat("\n")
cat("Criteria 1: Small overfitting (shrinkage effect >= 90%)\n")
cat("Criteria 2: Small R-squared difference (apparent - adjusted <= 0.05 Nagelkerke)\n")
cat("Criteria 3: Precise outcome risk estimation (margin of error <= 0.05)\n")
cat("Final: Maximum required sample size across all criteria\n")

# Prepare output for POWER_AGENT_RESULT
results_output <- data.frame(
  metric = c("sample_size", "n_events", "prevalence", "parameters", 
             "anticipated_cs_r2", "outcome_risk_margin_of_error"),
  value = c(min_sample_size, n_events, prevalence, parameters, cs_r2, margin_of_error),
  unit = c("participants_total", "events", "proportion", "count", 
           "proportion", "absolute_difference")
)

print(results_output)

# ME = z_{α/2} * sqrt[p(1-p)/n]
# where p = outcome prevalence (expected risk)

z_alpha_2 <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)

# Calculate achieved margin of error
achieved_moe <- z_alpha_2 * sqrt(prevalence * (1 - prevalence) / n_total)

plan.estimand: Minimum total sample size for binary prediction model development meeting Riley precision criteria
plan.hypothesis: Development of a multivariable prediction model with 10 candidate predictors should achieve shrinkage-adjusted discrimination and calibration meeting specified precision thresholds
assumptions: Binary logistic regression prediction model with multivariable coefficients estimated via maximum likelihood
10 candidate predictors will be included in the model with potential for shrinkage to address overfitting
Anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared of 0.12 represents expected discrimination after accounting for shrinkage
Shrinkage factor of 0.95 represents expected post-hoc shrinkage or uniform shrinkage of coefficients
Default Riley precision criteria: (i) absolute difference between apparent and adjusted R-squared (Nagelkerke scale) ≤ 0.05 for calibration; (ii) average predicted outcome risk margin of error ≤ 0.05
Two-stage precision framework: overfitting control via discrimination-based calculation; calibration verification via outcome-risk margin
Normal approximation for confidence intervals in derivation cohort without external validation
scientific_notes: Riley et al. (2020, 2021) framework targets multivariable binary prediction model development in a derivation cohort
Sample size accounts for overfitting penalty: apparent (training) discrimination typically exceeds adjusted (cross-validated or shrinkage-corrected) discrimination
Cox-Snell R-squared commonly used for survival models; pmsampsize 1.1.3 binary mode uses this as key discrimination measure
Shrinkage factor 0.95 suggests moderate penalty (5% shrinkage); typical uniform shrinkage factors range 0.8–1.0
Precision criteria are absolute thresholds, not relative; outcome-risk calibration addressed via margin of error on predicted probabilities
Default pmsampsize behavior: calculate discrimination-driven sample size, then verify via outcome-risk margin at returned N

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

       shrinkage = 0.9,

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

library(pmsampsize)

# Riley binary development criteria
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "b",              
  csrsquared = 0.12,       
  parameters = 10,         
  prevalence = 0.20,       
  shrinkage = 0.95         
)

# Extract key results
min_sample_size <- result$sample_size
n_events <- result$events
prevalence <- result$prevalence
parameters <- result$parameters
cs_r2 <- result$rsquared
nag_r2 <- result$nag_r2
epp <- result$EPP
final_shrinkage <- result$final_shrinkage

cat("=== RILEY BINARY PREDICTION MODEL DEVELOPMENT ===\n\n")
cat("PRIMARY RESULT:\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size required:", min_sample_size, "participants\n")
cat("Number of events:", n_events, "\n")
cat("Number of non-events:", min_sample_size - n_events, "\n\n")

cat("MODEL SPECIFICATION:\n")
cat("Number of candidate predictor parameters:", parameters, "\n")
cat("Outcome prevalence:", prevalence, "\n")
cat("Anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared:", cs_r2, "\n")
cat("Nagelkerke R-squared (on 0-1 scale):", nag_r2, "\n")
cat("Final shrinkage factor:", final_shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Events per Parameter (EPP):", round(epp, 2), "\n\n")

# Verify outcome-risk precision (Criterion 3)
# For binary models, the margin of error in outcome risk estimation is:
# ME = z_{alpha/2} * sqrt(p(1-p)/n)
# where p is prevalence and n is sample size
# Target margin of error = 0.05 (user-specified)

z_alpha_2 <- qnorm(1 - 0.05/2)  # 95% CI, two-sided
margin_of_error <- z_alpha_2 * sqrt(prevalence * (1 - prevalence) / min_sample_size)

cat("OUTCOME-RISK PRECISION VERIFICATION (Criterion 3):\n")
cat("Z-critical value (95% CI):", round(z_alpha_2, 4), "\n")
cat("Calculated absolute margin of error in average outcome risk:", 
    round(margin_of_error, 4), "\n")
cat("Target margin of error (from user):", 0.05, "\n")
cat("Criterion met (MoE <= 0.05)?:", 
    ifelse(margin_of_error <= 0.05, "YES", "NO"), "\n\n")

# Verify discrimination/calibration precision (Criterion 2)
# The difference between apparent and adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared should be <= 0.05
# This is implicit in the calculation, as pmsampsize uses shrinkage to estimate this

cat("DISCRIMINATION/CALIBRATION PRECISION (Criterion 2):\n")
cat("Difference threshold (Nagelkerke R-squared):", 0.05, "\n")
cat("NB: pmsampsize ensures this via shrinkage factor specification\n\n")

# Results table summary
cat("CRITERIA SUMMARY TABLE:\n")
print(result$results_table)

cat("\n")
cat("Criteria 1: Small overfitting (shrinkage effect >= 90%)\n")
cat("Criteria 2: Small R-squared difference (apparent - adjusted <= 0.05 Nagelkerke)\n")
cat("Criteria 3: Precise outcome risk estimation (margin of error <= 0.05)\n")
cat("Final: Maximum required sample size across all criteria\n")

# Prepare output for POWER_AGENT_RESULT
results_output <- data.frame(
  metric = c("sample_size", "n_events", "prevalence", "parameters", 
             "anticipated_cs_r2", "outcome_risk_margin_of_error"),
  value = c(min_sample_size, n_events, prevalence, parameters, cs_r2, margin_of_error),
  unit = c("participants_total", "events", "proportion", "count", 
           "proportion", "absolute_difference")
)

print(results_output)

  results = list(

# Detailed verification of outcome-risk precision criterion
cat("=== DETAILED OUTCOME-RISK PRECISION VERIFICATION ===\n\n")

# Parameters
prevalence <- 0.20
n_total <- 1482
confidence_level <- 0.95
alpha <- 1 - confidence_level
target_moe <- 0.05

# Margin of error formula for binomial proportion (outcome risk)
# ME = z_{α/2} * sqrt[p(1-p)/n]
# where p = outcome prevalence (expected risk)

z_alpha_2 <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)

# Calculate achieved margin of error
achieved_moe <- z_alpha_2 * sqrt(prevalence * (1 - prevalence) / n_total)

cat("Confidence level:", confidence_level * 100, "%\n")
cat("Alpha (two-tailed):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Z-critical value (α/2):", round(z_alpha_2, 6), "\n")
cat("Outcome prevalence (p):", prevalence, "\n")
cat("Total sample size (N):", n_total, "\n\n")

cat("Margin of error calculation:\n")
cat("ME = z_{α/2} × √[p(1-p)/n]\n")
cat("ME =", round(z_alpha_2, 4), "× √[", prevalence, "×", 1-prevalence, "/", n_total, "]\n")
cat("ME =", round(z_alpha_2, 4), "× √[", prevalence * (1 - prevalence), "/", n_total, "]\n")
cat("ME =", round(z_alpha_2, 4), "× √[", 
    round(prevalence * (1 - prevalence) / n_total, 8), "]\n")
cat("ME =", round(z_alpha_2, 4), "×", 
    round(sqrt(prevalence * (1 - prevalence) / n_total), 8), "\n")
cat("ME =", round(achieved_moe, 6), "\n\n")

cat("Target margin of error (user-specified):", target_moe, "\n")
cat("Achieved margin of error:", round(achieved_moe, 6), "\n")
cat("Achieved <= Target?:", achieved_moe <= target_moe, "\n\n")

# Express as confidence interval for outcome risk
ci_lower <- prevalence - achieved_moe
ci_upper <- prevalence + achieved_moe

cat("Confidence interval for average outcome risk (average probability):\n")
cat("Point estimate (expected prevalence):", prevalence, "\n")
cat("95% CI: [", round(ci_lower, 4), ",", round(ci_upper, 4), "]\n")
cat("CI width (±):", round(achieved_moe, 4), "\n\n")

# Verify against default criterion: 0.05
cat("Default Riley criterion for outcome-risk precision: MOE ≤ 0.05\n")
cat("Criterion met:", achieved_moe <= 0.05, "\n\n")

# Check the candidate's reported value
reported_moe <- 0.0204
cat("Candidate reported margin of error:", reported_moe, "\n")
cat("Independently calculated margin of error:", round(achieved_moe, 4), "\n")
cat("Exact match:", round(achieved_moe, 4) == reported_moe, "\n")

# For binary models, the margin of error in outcome risk estimation is:
# ME = z_{alpha/2} * sqrt(p(1-p)/n)
# where p is prevalence and n is sample size
# Target margin of error = 0.05 (user-specified)

z_alpha_2 <- qnorm(1 - 0.05/2)  # 95% CI, two-sided
margin_of_error <- z_alpha_2 * sqrt(prevalence * (1 - prevalence) / min_sample_size)

cat("OUTCOME-RISK PRECISION VERIFICATION (Criterion 3):\n")
cat("Z-critical value (95% CI):", round(z_alpha_2, 4), "\n")
cat("Calculated absolute margin of error in average outcome risk:", 
    round(margin_of_error, 4), "\n")
cat("Target margin of error (from user):", 0.05, "\n")
cat("Criterion met (MoE <= 0.05)?:", 
    ifelse(margin_of_error <= 0.05, "YES", "NO"), "\n\n")

# Verify discrimination/calibration precision (Criterion 2)
# The difference between apparent and adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared should be <= 0.05
# This is implicit in the calculation, as pmsampsize uses shrinkage to estimate this

cat("DISCRIMINATION/CALIBRATION PRECISION (Criterion 2):\n")
cat("Difference threshold (Nagelkerke R-squared):", 0.05, "\n")
cat("NB: pmsampsize ensures this via shrinkage factor specification\n\n")

# Results table summary
cat("CRITERIA SUMMARY TABLE:\n")
print(result$results_table)

cat("\n")
cat("Criteria 1: Small overfitting (shrinkage effect >= 90%)\n")
cat("Criteria 2: Small R-squared difference (apparent - adjusted <= 0.05 Nagelkerke)\n")
cat("Criteria 3: Precise outcome risk estimation (margin of error <= 0.05)\n")
cat("Final: Maximum required sample size across all criteria\n")

# Prepare output for POWER_AGENT_RESULT
results_output <- data.frame(
  metric = c("sample_size", "n_events", "prevalence", "parameters", 
             "anticipated_cs_r2", "outcome_risk_margin_of_error"),
  value = c(min_sample_size, n_events, prevalence, parameters, cs_r2, margin_of_error),
  unit = c("participants_total", "events", "proportion", "count", 
           "proportion", "absolute_difference")
)

print(results_output)

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

# One-way fixed effects ANOVA power calculation
# Design: 3 independent groups, balanced, common variance
# Total N = 75 (n = 25 per group)
# Population eta-squared = 0.08
# Significance level alpha = 0.05

# Parameters
k <- 3              # number of groups
N <- 75             # total sample size
n <- N / k          # per-group sample size
eta_sq <- 0.08      # population eta-squared
alpha <- 0.05       # significance level

# Derive noncentrality parameter from eta-squared
# The relationship is: eta_sq = lambda / (lambda + N - k)
# Solving for lambda: lambda = N * k * eta_sq / (1 - eta_sq)
# However, more directly: lambda = (1/n) * [sum of (mu_i - grand_mean)^2] * N / sigma^2
# For eta_sq: eta_sq = SS_between / SS_total = lambda / (lambda + N - k)
# Rearranging: lambda = eta_sq * (N - k) / (1 - eta_sq)

lambda <- eta_sq * (N - k) / (1 - eta_sq)

cat("Design Parameters:\n")
cat("Number of groups (k):", k, "\n")
cat("Total sample size (N):", N, "\n")
cat("Sample size per group (n):", n, "\n")
cat("Population eta-squared:", eta_sq, "\n")
cat("Significance level (alpha):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Noncentrality parameter (lambda):", lambda, "\n\n")

# Degrees of freedom
df_num <- k - 1         # numerator df
df_den <- N - k         # denominator df

cat("Degrees of freedom:\n")
cat("Numerator df (k-1):", df_num, "\n")
cat("Denominator df (N-k):", df_den, "\n\n")

# Critical F value at alpha = 0.05
F_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df_num, df_den)

cat("Critical F value at alpha =", alpha, ":\n")
cat("F_crit =", F_crit, "\n\n")

# Power: P(F > F_crit | H_1 true) using noncentral F distribution
# The noncentral F distribution with noncentrality parameter lambda
power <- 1 - pf(F_crit, df_num, df_den, ncp = lambda)

cat("Power Calculation:\n")
cat("Power = P(F > F_crit | H_1) =", power, "\n")

# Format result
results <- data.frame(
  metric = "power",
  value = power,
  unit = "probability"
)

library(jsonlite)
POWER_AGENT_RESULT <- paste0("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=", 
  toJSON(list(results = results), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))
cat("\n", POWER_AGENT_RESULT, "\n")

eta_sq <- 0.08

# Method 1: Direct calculation from eta_sq
# eta_sq = lambda / (lambda + N - k) where lambda is effect parameter
# Solving: eta_sq * (lambda + N - k) = lambda
#          eta_sq * lambda + eta_sq * (N - k) = lambda
#          eta_sq * (N - k) = lambda * (1 - eta_sq)
#          lambda = eta_sq * (N - k) / (1 - eta_sq)

lambda_method1 <- eta_sq * (N - k) / (1 - eta_sq)

# Cross-check: Verify eta_sq from lambda
eta_sq_check <- lambda_method1 / (lambda_method1 + N - k)

cat("Verification of eta-squared transformation:\n")
cat("Original eta-squared:", eta_sq, "\n")
cat("Computed noncentrality parameter (lambda):", lambda_method1, "\n")
cat("Recovered eta-squared from lambda:", eta_sq_check, "\n")

# The issue: there are different parameterizations of effect size for ANOVA
# eta^2 (proportion of variance explained) vs. Cohen's f (standardized effect)
#
# Relationship: f = sqrt(eta^2 / (1 - eta^2))
#              eta^2 = f^2 / (1 + f^2)
#
# Noncentrality parameter lambda in F-distribution:
# lambda = n * k * f^2 where this uses Cohen's f definition
# BUT the eta^2 definition relates to the population effect as:
# eta^2 = SS_between / SS_total
# In the population model where treatments have effects tau_i with sum(tau_i) = 0:
# eta^2 = sum(tau_i^2) / (k * sigma^2)
# and f^2 = eta^2 / (1 - eta^2) comes from a standardization

k <- 3
N <- 75
n <- N / k
eta_sq <- 0.08
alpha <- 0.05

# The correct noncentrality parameter for one-way ANOVA is:
# lambda = (1/sigma^2) * n * sum_i(mu_i - mu_grand)^2
# When expressed in terms of eta^2 in the population:
# eta^2 = sum_i(mu_i - mu_grand)^2 / (k * sigma^2)  [among-group variance ratio]
# Therefore: lambda = n * k * eta^2 / (1 - eta^2) ... this is what we used

lambda_correct <- n * k * eta_sq / (1 - eta_sq)

# Now let's see the relationship with f
# Cohen's f = sqrt(eta^2 / (1 - eta^2))
# So: f^2 = eta^2 / (1 - eta^2)
# and lambda = n * k * f^2 = n * k * eta^2 / (1 - eta^2) ✓

f_cohen <- sqrt(eta_sq / (1 - eta_sq))
lambda_via_f <- n * k * f_cohen^2

cat("Clarification of Effect Size Parameterization:\n")
cat("eta^2 (population):", eta_sq, "\n")

cat("f^2:", f_cohen^2, "\n")

cat("Noncentrality Parameter:\n")

cat("lambda (via f):", lambda_via_f, "\n")
cat("Match:", isTRUE(all.equal(lambda_correct, lambda_via_f, tolerance = 1e-10)), "\n\n")

# The discrepancy noted earlier was likely due to a typo in my verification code.
# Let me recalculate everything cleanly.

df_num <- k - 1
df_den <- N - k
F_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df_num, df_den)

# The key issue: eta-squared can be defined in two ways in ANOVA power calculations
# 1. Proportion of variance explained: eta^2 = SS_B / SS_T where this is observed
# 2. Effect size parameter in the population model
#
# For power calculation, we need the population effect size.
# Standard reference: Cohen's (1988) power analysis for ANOVA
#
# Cohen defines f (effect size) for ANOVA as:
# f = sqrt[ sum_i (mu_i - mu_grand)^2 ] / (k * sigma^2)
# which is the square root of the ratio of among-group variance to error variance
#
# The noncentrality parameter is:
# lambda = n * k * f^2 = n * sum_i(mu_i - mu_grand)^2 / sigma^2
#
# Now, eta^2 (as a population parameter) relates to f by:
# eta^2 = f^2 / (1 + f^2)  [alternative definition used in some contexts]
# OR
# eta^2 = SS_B / SS_T = omega^2 in large samples
#
# The more direct approach: given eta^2 as the problem states it,
# we need to clarify what it means.
#
# INTERPRETATION 1: eta^2 is the population correlation ratio
# eta^2 = sum_i[n_i(mu_i - mu)^2] / (n*sigma^2_total)
# For fixed effects ANOVA: eta^2 = lambda / (lambda + k*(N-k))
#
# INTERPRETATION 2 (Cohen's f-based): 
# f = sqrt(eta^2 / (1 - eta^2)) is standard ANOVA interpretation

# One-way fixed effects ANOVA power calculation
# Design: 3 independent groups, balanced, common variance
# Total N = 75 (n = 25 per group)
# Population eta-squared = 0.08
# Significance level alpha = 0.05

# Parameters
k <- 3              # number of groups
N <- 75             # total sample size
n <- N / k          # per-group sample size
eta_sq <- 0.08      # population eta-squared
alpha <- 0.05       # significance level

# Derive noncentrality parameter from eta-squared
# The relationship is: eta_sq = lambda / (lambda + N - k)
# Solving for lambda: lambda = N * k * eta_sq / (1 - eta_sq)
# However, more directly: lambda = (1/n) * [sum of (mu_i - grand_mean)^2] * N / sigma^2
# For eta_sq: eta_sq = SS_between / SS_total = lambda / (lambda + N - k)
# Rearranging: lambda = eta_sq * (N - k) / (1 - eta_sq)

lambda <- eta_sq * (N - k) / (1 - eta_sq)

cat("Design Parameters:\n")
cat("Number of groups (k):", k, "\n")
cat("Total sample size (N):", N, "\n")
cat("Sample size per group (n):", n, "\n")
cat("Population eta-squared:", eta_sq, "\n")
cat("Significance level (alpha):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Noncentrality parameter (lambda):", lambda, "\n\n")

# Degrees of freedom
df_num <- k - 1         # numerator df
df_den <- N - k         # denominator df

cat("Degrees of freedom:\n")
cat("Numerator df (k-1):", df_num, "\n")
cat("Denominator df (N-k):", df_den, "\n\n")

# Critical F value at alpha = 0.05
F_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df_num, df_den)

cat("Critical F value at alpha =", alpha, ":\n")
cat("F_crit =", F_crit, "\n\n")

# Power: P(F > F_crit | H_1 true) using noncentral F distribution
# The noncentral F distribution with noncentrality parameter lambda
power <- 1 - pf(F_crit, df_num, df_den, ncp = lambda)

cat("Power Calculation:\n")
cat("Power = P(F > F_crit | H_1) =", power, "\n")

# Format result
results <- data.frame(
  metric = "power",
  value = power,
  unit = "probability"
)

library(jsonlite)
POWER_AGENT_RESULT <- paste0("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=", 
  toJSON(list(results = results), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))
cat("\n", POWER_AGENT_RESULT, "\n")

# The key issue: eta-squared can be defined in two ways in ANOVA power calculations
# 1. Proportion of variance explained: eta^2 = SS_B / SS_T where this is observed
# 2. Effect size parameter in the population model
#
# For power calculation, we need the population effect size.
# Standard reference: Cohen's (1988) power analysis for ANOVA
#
# Cohen defines f (effect size) for ANOVA as:
# f = sqrt[ sum_i (mu_i - mu_grand)^2 ] / (k * sigma^2)
# which is the square root of the ratio of among-group variance to error variance
#
# The noncentrality parameter is:
# lambda = n * k * f^2 = n * sum_i(mu_i - mu_grand)^2 / sigma^2
#
# Now, eta^2 (as a population parameter) relates to f by:
# eta^2 = f^2 / (1 + f^2)  [alternative definition used in some contexts]
# OR
# eta^2 = SS_B / SS_T = omega^2 in large samples
#
# The more direct approach: given eta^2 as the problem states it,
# we need to clarify what it means.
#
# INTERPRETATION 1: eta^2 is the population correlation ratio
# eta^2 = sum_i[n_i(mu_i - mu)^2] / (n*sigma^2_total)
# For fixed effects ANOVA: eta^2 = lambda / (lambda + k*(N-k))
#
# INTERPRETATION 2 (Cohen's f-based): 
# f = sqrt(eta^2 / (1 - eta^2)) is standard ANOVA interpretation
#
# Let me check which interpretation gives sensible results using pwr package

library(pwr)

# Parameters
k <- 3
N <- 75
n <- N / k
eta_sq_given <- 0.08
alpha <- 0.05

# Evidence e1; success=true

# One-way fixed effects ANOVA power calculation
# Design: 3 independent groups, balanced, common variance
# Total N = 75 (n = 25 per group)
# Population eta-squared = 0.08
# Significance level alpha = 0.05

# Parameters
k <- 3              # number of groups
N <- 75             # total sample size
n <- N / k          # per-group sample size
eta_sq <- 0.08      # population eta-squared
alpha <- 0.05       # significance level

# Derive noncentrality parameter from eta-squared
# The relationship is: eta_sq = lambda / (lambda + N - k)
# Solving for lambda: lambda = N * k * eta_sq / (1 - eta_sq)
# However, more directly: lambda = (1/n) * [sum of (mu_i - grand_mean)^2] * N / sigma^2
# For eta_sq: eta_sq = SS_between / SS_total = lambda / (lambda + N - k)
# Rearranging: lambda = eta_sq * (N - k) / (1 - eta_sq)

lambda <- eta_sq * (N - k) / (1 - eta_sq)

cat("Design Parameters:\n")
cat("Number of groups (k):", k, "\n")
cat("Total sample size (N):", N, "\n")
cat("Sample size per group (n):", n, "\n")
cat("Population eta-squared:", eta_sq, "\n")
cat("Significance level (alpha):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Noncentrality parameter (lambda):", lambda, "\n\n")

# Degrees of freedom
df_num <- k - 1         # numerator df
df_den <- N - k         # denominator df

cat("Degrees of freedom:\n")
cat("Numerator df (k-1):", df_num, "\n")
cat("Denominator df (N-k):", df_den, "\n\n")

# Critical F value at alpha = 0.05
F_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df_num, df_den)

cat("Critical F value at alpha =", alpha, ":\n")
cat("F_crit =", F_crit, "\n\n")

# Power: P(F > F_crit | H_1 true) using noncentral F distribution
# The noncentral F distribution with noncentrality parameter lambda
power <- 1 - pf(F_crit, df_num, df_den, ncp = lambda)

cat("Power Calculation:\n")
cat("Power = P(F > F_crit | H_1) =", power, "\n")

# Format result
results <- data.frame(
  metric = "power",
  value = power,
  unit = "probability"
)

library(jsonlite)
POWER_AGENT_RESULT <- paste0("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=", 
  toJSON(list(results = results), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))
cat("\n", POWER_AGENT_RESULT, "\n")

N <- 75
n <- N / k

alpha <- 0.05

# Method 1: Direct calculation from eta_sq
# eta_sq = lambda / (lambda + N - k) where lambda is effect parameter
# Solving: eta_sq * (lambda + N - k) = lambda
#          eta_sq * lambda + eta_sq * (N - k) = lambda
#          eta_sq * (N - k) = lambda * (1 - eta_sq)
#          lambda = eta_sq * (N - k) / (1 - eta_sq)

lambda_method1 <- eta_sq * (N - k) / (1 - eta_sq)

# Cross-check: Verify eta_sq from lambda
eta_sq_check <- lambda_method1 / (lambda_method1 + N - k)

cat("Verification of eta-squared transformation:\n")
cat("Original eta-squared:", eta_sq, "\n")
cat("Computed noncentrality parameter (lambda):", lambda_method1, "\n")
cat("Recovered eta-squared from lambda:", eta_sq_check, "\n")
cat("Match:", isTRUE(all.equal(eta_sq, eta_sq_check, tolerance = 1e-10)), "\n\n")

# In some references, the effect size is expressed as f = sqrt(eta_sq / (1 - eta_sq))
# and lambda = n * k * f^2
f <- sqrt(eta_sq / (1 - eta_sq))

cat("Cohen's f =", f, "\n")
cat("Lambda via f =", lambda_method2, "\n")

df_den <- N - k

power_final <- 1 - pf(F_crit, df_num, df_den, ncp = lambda_method1)

cat("Noncentrality parameter:", lambda_method1, "\n")
cat("Power (omnibus F-test):", sprintf("%.10f", power_final), "\n")

# Therefore: lambda = n * k * eta^2 / (1 - eta^2) ... this is what we used

# So: f^2 = eta^2 / (1 - eta^2)
# and lambda = n * k * f^2 = n * k * eta^2 / (1 - eta^2) ✓

cat("Cohen's f:", f_cohen, "\n")
cat("f^2:", f_cohen^2, "\n")

cat("Noncentrality Parameter:\n")
cat("lambda (direct from eta^2):", lambda_correct, "\n")
cat("lambda (via f):", lambda_via_f, "\n")
cat("Match:", isTRUE(all.equal(lambda_correct, lambda_via_f, tolerance = 1e-10)), "\n\n")

# The discrepancy noted earlier was likely due to a typo in my verification code.
# Let me recalculate everything cleanly.

df_num <- k - 1
df_den <- N - k
F_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df_num, df_den)
power <- 1 - pf(F_crit, df_num, df_den, ncp = lambda_correct)

cat("FINAL POWER CALCULATION:\n")
cat("========================================\n")
cat("Design: One-way ANOVA, balanced\n")
cat("Number of groups:", k, "\n")
cat("Sample per group:", n, "\n")
cat("Total N:", N, "\n")
cat("Population eta-squared:", eta_sq, "\n")

cat("Eta-squared (η²):", eta_sq, "\n")

cat("Numerator df:", df_num, "\n")
cat("Denominator df:", df_den, "\n")
cat("Critical F-value:", sprintf("%.10f", F_crit), "\n")
cat("Noncentrality parameter λ:", sprintf("%.10f", lambda_correct), "\n\n")

cat("POWER:", sprintf("%.10f", power), "\n")

  toJSON(list(results = list(list(metric = "power", value = power, unit = "probability"))), 
    auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))
cat("\n", POWER_AGENT_RESULT, "\n")

answer.summary: For a one-sided one-sample t-test comparing a normally distributed outcome with a mean increase of 0.2 units (SD 0.5) against a null mean of 0, the minimum sample size to achieve 80% power at α = 0.05 is **41 participants**. This achieves an actual power of 80.86%, exceeding the 80% target. At the preceding sample size (n = 40), power is 79.97%, confirming that 41 is the minimum integer sample size meeting the power specification.
answer.method: One-sample t-test power calculation via the R package pwr (version 1.3-0), which inverts the noncentral t-distribution CDF. The effect size is Cohen's d = (μ₁ − μ₀) / σ = 0.2 / 0.5 = 0.4. Calculation uses the exact noncentral t-distribution parameterized by degrees of freedom (n − 1), noncentrality λ = √n × d, and critical value from t(α, n−1). Sample size is determined by finding the smallest integer n such that power(n, d, α) ≥ 0.80.
assumptions: Outcome is normally distributed with mean μ and constant variance σ² = (0.5)²
Null hypothesis: μ = 0; alternative hypothesis: μ > 0 (one-sided, superiority)
Single sample of independent observations, each measured once
Test statistic t = (X̄ − 0) / (S / √n) follows t(n−1) under H₀
Significance level α = 0.05 (one-sided)
No multiple testing, no interim analyses, no multiplicity adjustment
limitations: Power calculation assumes the normal approximation is adequate; for small samples (n < 30) validity depends on underlying normality.
Effect size (d = 0.4) is assumed known and constant; sample size does not account for uncertainty in estimation of σ.
No attrition or dropout is modeled; achieved sample size must remain at n = 41 for claimed power.
One-sided test increases power relative to two-sided; direction of effect must be specified a priori.
Calculation does not address issues such as measurement error, confounding, or model misspecification beyond the specified t-test framework.

executions.code:
# One-sample t-test power and sample size calculation
# H0: μ = 0 vs H1: μ = 0.2 (one-sided)
# Effect: mean increase 0.2 units, SD = 0.5
# Alpha = 0.05, target power = 0.8

library(pwr)

# Parameters
mean_diff <- 0.2    # Effect size in original units
sd <- 0.5           # Standard deviation
cohen_d <- mean_diff / sd  # Effect size (Cohen's d)
alpha <- 0.05       # Significance level (one-sided)
target_power <- 0.80  # Target power

cat("Study Design: One-Sample t-Test\n")
cat("H0: μ = 0 vs H1: μ > 0 (one-sided)\n")
cat("Mean difference:", mean_diff, "units\n")
cat("Standard deviation:", sd, "units\n")
cat("Cohen's d:", cohen_d, "\n")
cat("Alpha (one-sided):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n\n")

# Calculate minimum sample size for target power = 0.80
# pwr.t.test uses d = effect size (Cohen's d), n = sample size per group (for one-sample, n is total)
n_continuous <- pwr.t.test(d = cohen_d, sig.level = alpha, power = target_power, 
                           type = "one.sample", alternative = "greater")$n

cat("Continuous solution (one-sided):", n_continuous, "participants\n")

# Round up to nearest integer
n_integer <- ceiling(n_continuous)

cat("Minimum integer sample size:", n_integer, "participants\n\n")

# Verify achieved power at the recommended sample size
power_at_n <- pwr.t.test(n = n_integer, d = cohen_d, sig.level = alpha, 
                         type = "one.sample", alternative = "greater")$power

cat("Achieved power at n =", n_integer, ":", power_at_n, "\n")

# Also check power at n-1 to confirm this is the minimum
if (n_integer > 1) {
  power_at_n_minus_1 <- pwr.t.test(n = n_integer - 1, d = cohen_d, sig.level = alpha, 
                                   type = "one.sample", alternative = "greater")$power
  cat("Power at n =", n_integer - 1, ":", power_at_n_minus_1, "\n")
  cat("\nConfirmation: n =", n_integer, "is the minimum integer achieving target power\n")
}

# Store result for reporting
result_n <- n_integer
result_power <- power_at_n

# One-way ANOVA power and sample size calculation
# H0: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ vs H1: at least one group mean differs
# Design: balanced, 3 independent normal groups, common variance
# Population eta-squared = 0.06, target power = 0.80, alpha = 0.05

# Relationship between eta-squared and noncentral F parameter
# η² = λ / (λ + N) where λ is the noncentrality parameter and N is total sample size
# Rearranging: λ = η² * N / (1 - η²)

# Parameters
k <- 3              # number of groups
eta_sq <- 0.06      # population eta-squared
alpha <- 0.05       # significance level
target_power <- 0.80
df1 <- k - 1        # numerator degrees of freedom = 2
# df2 = N - k = n*k - k, where n is per-group sample size

# Critical F-value for α = 0.05, df1 = 2
f_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df1, Inf)  # using infinite denominator df as approximation initially
cat("Critical F-value (df1=2, alpha=0.05):", f_crit, "\n\n")

# Function to compute power given sample size per group
compute_power <- function(n_per_group, k, eta_sq, alpha) {
  N_total <- n_per_group * k
  df2 <- N_total - k
  
  # Noncentrality parameter λ
  lambda <- eta_sq * N_total / (1 - eta_sq)
  
  # Critical F value
  f_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, k - 1, df2)
  
  # Power = P(F > f_crit | H1)
  power <- 1 - pf(f_crit, k - 1, df2, ncp = lambda)
  
  return(list(n_per_group = n_per_group, N_total = N_total, lambda = lambda, 
              df1 = k - 1, df2 = df2, f_crit = f_crit, power = power))
}

# Search for minimum n per group yielding power >= 0.80
# Start with reasonable range
n_range <- seq(50, 150, by = 5)
power_results <- lapply(n_range, function(n) compute_power(n, k, eta_sq, alpha))

# Extract powers
powers <- sapply(power_results, function(x) x$power)

# Display results
results_df <- data.frame(
  n_per_group = sapply(power_results, function(x) x$n_per_group),
  N_total = sapply(power_results, function(x) x$N_total),
  lambda = sapply(power_results, function(x) x$lambda),
  f_crit = sapply(power_results, function(x) x$f_crit),
  power = sapply(power_results, function(x) x$power)
)

cat("Coarse search (by 5):\n")
print(results_df)
cat("\n")

# Identify candidates near 0.80
idx_target <- which(powers >= target_power)
if (length(idx_target) > 0) {
  min_idx <- min(idx_target)
  candidate_n <- n_range[min_idx]
  cat("Candidate n per group (from coarse search):", candidate_n, "\n")
  
  # Refine search around the candidate
  n_fine <- seq(max(10, candidate_n - 10), candidate_n + 5)
  power_fine <- sapply(n_fine, function(n) compute_power(n, k, eta_sq, alpha)$power)
  
  fine_df <- data.frame(n_per_group = n_fine, power = power_fine)
  cat("\nFine search around candidate:\n")
  print(fine_df)
  
  # Find minimum n where power >= 0.80
  idx_min <- which(power_fine >= target_power)
  if (length(idx_min) > 0) {
    min_n_achieved <- n_fine[min(idx_min)]
    
    cat("\n=== RESULTS ===\n")
    cat("Minimum n per group achieving power >= 0.80:", min_n_achieved, "\n")
    
    # Compute detailed results for selected n
    selected <- compute_power(min_n_achieved, k, eta_sq, alpha)
    preceding <- compute_power(min_n_achieved - 1, k, eta_sq, alpha)
    
    cat("\nSelected design (n =", min_n_achieved, "):\n")
    cat("  Total sample size:", selected$N_total, "\n")
    cat("  Noncentrality parameter λ:", round(selected$lambda, 4), "\n")
    cat("  Critical F-value (df1=", selected$df1, ", df2=", selected$df2, "):", 
        round(selected$f_crit, 4), "\n")
    cat("  Achieved power:", round(selected$power, 4), "\n")
    
    cat("\nPreceding design (n =", min_n_achieved - 1, "):\n")
    cat("  Total sample size:", preceding$N_total, "\n")
    cat("  Noncentrality parameter λ:", round(preceding$lambda, 4), "\n")
    cat("  Critical F-value (df1=", preceding$df1, ", df2=", preceding$df2, "):", 
        round(preceding$f_crit, 4), "\n")
    cat("  Achieved power:", round(preceding$power, 4), "\n")
    
    cat("\n=== FINAL ANSWER ===\n")
    cat("Minimum integer participants per group:", min_n_achieved, "\n")
    cat("Achieved power:", round(selected$power, 4), "\n")
    cat("Power at preceding design (n =", min_n_achieved - 1, "):", round(preceding$power, 4), "\n")
  }
}

# Export result as JSON
result_json <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = min_n_achieved, unit = "participants_per_group"),
    list(metric = "achieved_power", value = round(selected$power, 6), unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "power_at_preceding_design", value = round(preceding$power, 6), unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "total_sample_size", value = selected$N_total, unit = "participants"),
    list(metric = "noncentrality_parameter", value = round(selected$lambda, 6), unit = "dimensionless")
  )
)

cat("\n\nJSON Output:\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
jsonlite::toJSON(result_json, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15)

library(jsonlite)

# Set parameters
k <- 3
eta_sq <- 0.06
alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.80

# Verify the eta-squared to noncentrality relationship
# For one-way ANOVA, eta-squared is defined as:
# η² = SS_between / SS_total
# 
# Under the model with group means μ₁, ..., μₖ and common variance σ²,
# if we specify η² as the population effect size, the relationship to λ is:
# λ = f² * df2 / (1 - f²) where f is Cohen's f effect size
# But more directly for balanced designs:
# η² = λ / (λ + N) is the relationship between population eta-squared and λ
# Therefore: λ = η² * N / (1 - η²)

# Verify this with a specific example
N_test <- 156
lambda_test <- eta_sq * N_test / (1 - eta_sq)
eta_sq_back <- lambda_test / (lambda_test + N_test)

cat("Verification of eta-squared <-> noncentrality relationship:\n")
cat("N_total =", N_test, "\n")
cat("λ = η² * N / (1 - η²) =", eta_sq, "* ", N_test, "/", (1 - eta_sq), "=", lambda_test, "\n")
cat("η² back = λ / (λ + N) =", lambda_test, "/", (lambda_test + N_test), "=", eta_sq_back, "\n")
cat("Match:", isTRUE(all.equal(eta_sq_back, eta_sq)), "\n\n")

# Now compute power for n=52 (N=156)
n_selected <- 52
N_selected <- n_selected * k
df1 <- k - 1  # 2
df2 <- N_selected - k  # 153

lambda_selected <- eta_sq * N_selected / (1 - eta_sq)
f_crit_selected <- qf(1 - alpha, df1, df2)
power_selected <- 1 - pf(f_crit_selected, df1, df2, ncp = lambda_selected)

cat("=== Selected Design: n = 52 per group ===\n")
cat("Total N:", N_selected, "\n")
cat("df1:", df1, ", df2:", df2, "\n")
cat("λ:", round(lambda_selected, 6), "\n")
cat("Critical F-value:", round(f_crit_selected, 6), "\n")
cat("Power:", round(power_selected, 6), "\n\n")

# Verify the preceding design: n=51 (N=153)
n_preceding <- 51
N_preceding <- n_preceding * k
df2_preceding <- N_preceding - k  # 150

lambda_preceding <- eta_sq * N_preceding / (1 - eta_sq)
f_crit_preceding <- qf(1 - alpha, df1, df2_preceding)
power_preceding <- 1 - pf(f_crit_preceding, df1, df2_preceding, ncp = lambda_preceding)

cat("=== Preceding Design: n = 51 per group ===\n")
cat("Total N:", N_preceding, "\n")
cat("df1:", df1, ", df2:", df2_preceding, "\n")
cat("λ:", round(lambda_preceding, 6), "\n")
cat("Critical F-value:", round(f_crit_preceding, 6), "\n")
cat("Power:", round(power_preceding, 6), "\n\n")

# Verify minimum n by checking both sides
cat("=== Verification of minimum n ===\n")
for (n in 50:54) {
  N_temp <- n * k
  df2_temp <- N_temp - k
  lambda_temp <- eta_sq * N_temp / (1 - eta_sq)
  f_crit_temp <- qf(1 - alpha, df1, df2_temp)

cat("Minimum n per group achieving power ≥ 0.80: 52\n")
cat("Achieved power at n=52:", round(power_selected, 6), "\n")
cat("Power at n=51:", round(power_preceding, 6), "\n")

    list(metric = "achieved_power", value = round(power_selected, 6), unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "power_at_preceding_design", value = round(power_preceding, 6), unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "total_sample_size", value = N_selected, unit = "participants"),
    list(metric = "noncentrality_parameter", value = round(lambda_selected, 6), unit = "dimensionless")

# Cross-check: verify the eta-squared and noncentrality relationship using an 
# alternative formulation based on Cohen's f effect size

# Cohen's f effect size is related to eta-squared by:
# f = sqrt(η² / (1 - η²))
# η² = f² / (1 + f²)

# For a balanced one-way ANOVA with k groups and n per group (N = n*k total):
# The noncentrality parameter is λ = n * k * f² / (1 - f²) * (k - 1) / (k - 1)
# Which simplifies to: λ = N * f² / (1 - f²) = N * η² / (1 - η²)

library(jsonlite)

# Parameters
k <- 3
eta_sq <- 0.06
n_per_group <- 52
N_total <- n_per_group * k

# Compute Cohen's f from eta-squared
f <- sqrt(eta_sq / (1 - eta_sq))
eta_sq_check <- f^2 / (1 + f^2)

cat("=== Cohen's f Effect Size ===\n")
cat("Population η² =", eta_sq, "\n")
cat("Cohen's f = sqrt(η² / (1 - η²)) =", f, "\n")
cat("Verification: η² = f² / (1 + f²) =", eta_sq_check, "\n")
cat("Match:", isTRUE(all.equal(eta_sq, eta_sq_check)), "\n\n")

# Noncentrality parameter using Cohen's f
lambda_cohens_f <- N_total * f^2 / (1 - f^2)
lambda_direct <- eta_sq * N_total / (1 - eta_sq)

cat("=== Noncentrality Parameter ===\n")
cat("Using Cohen's f: λ = N * f² / (1 - f²) =", N_total, "*", f^2, "/", (1 - f^2), "=", lambda_cohens_f, "\n")
cat("Using η² directly: λ = η² * N / (1 - η²) =", eta_sq, "*", N_total, "/", (1 - eta_sq), "=", lambda_direct, "\n")
cat("Match:", isTRUE(all.equal(lambda_cohens_f, lambda_direct)), "\n\n")

# Power computation
df1 <- k - 1
df2 <- N_total - k
alpha <- 0.05
f_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df1, df2)

# Power from noncentral F
power <- 1 - pf(f_crit, df1, df2, ncp = lambda_direct)

cat("=== Power Computation ===\n")
cat("df1 (numerator) =", df1, "\n")
cat("df2 (denominator) =", df2, "\n")
cat("F-critical (α = 0.05) =", round(f_crit, 6), "\n")
cat("Noncentrality λ =", round(lambda_direct, 6), "\n")
cat("Power = P(F_noncentral > F_crit) =", round(power, 6), "\n\n")

# Also verify using pf with mean and variance of noncentral F
# For reference, showing that the noncentral F is correctly applied
mean_noncentral_f <- (df2 * (df1 + lambda_direct)) / (df2 - 2)
cat("Expected mean of noncentral F (for reference):", round(mean_noncentral_f, 4), "\n")
cat("(This is informational; power is computed directly from CDF)\n\n")

# Final summary
cat("=== FINAL VERIFICATION ===\n")
cat("Design: k =", k, "groups, n =", n_per_group, "per group, N =", N_total, "total\n")
cat("Effect size: η² =", eta_sq, "(Cohen's f =", round(f, 6), ")\n")
cat("Test: α =", alpha, ", df =", df1, "vs", df2, "\n")
cat("Result: Achieved power =", round(power, 6), "\n")
cat("Target power = 0.80, Achieved power >= Target?", power >= 0.80, "\n")

# Output for independent check
check_result <- list(
  design = "one_way_anova",
  parameters = list(
    k_groups = k,
    n_per_group = n_per_group,
    N_total = N_total,
    eta_squared = eta_sq,
    cohens_f = f,
    alpha = alpha
  ),
  noncentrality = list(
    lambda = lambda_direct,
    lambda_from_cohens_f = lambda_cohens_f,
    match = isTRUE(all.equal(lambda_direct, lambda_cohens_f))
  ),
  power_computation = list(
    df1 = df1,
    df2 = df2,
    f_critical = f_crit,
    power = power,
    meets_target = power >= 0.80
  )
)

cat("\nJSON Check Result:\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(toJSON(check_result, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))
