plan.estimand: Development sample size for internal validation of a continuous prediction model meeting Riley criteria for model performance stability
plan.hypothesis: The fitted model will meet combined precision criteria: (1) shrinkage of true adjusted R² of at least 0.90 (i.e., ≤10% relative shrinkage), (2) maximum absolute difference between apparent and adjusted R² ≤ 0.05 on Nagelkerke scale, (3) residual SD multiplicative margin of error ≤ 1.1, and (4) outcome mean multiplicative margin of error ≤ 1.1, under 95% confidence.

parameters.name: residual SD multiplicative margin of error
outcome mean multiplicative margin of error

assumptions: Continuous outcome modeled with ordinary least squares (OLS) regression
Internal validation only; shrinkage criterion applies to adjusted R² relative to apparent R²
Precision criteria address margin of error for residual SD, outcome mean, and intercept at 95% confidence
Maximum acceptable absolute difference between apparent and adjusted R² is 0.05 on Nagelkerke scale
Model includes linear terms for all 25 candidate predictors; no variable selection post-hoc multiple testing accounted separately
pmsampsize 1.1.3 analytic formulation (Riley et al.) used; implementation assumes standard OLS assumptions (normality of residuals conditional on predictors)
Sample size calculated to meet the most stringent binding constraint among shrinkage, R² difference, and margin-of-error criteria
scientific_notes: Riley et al. criteria for prediction model development balance overfitting (shrinkage criterion) against precision of intercept, outcome mean, and residual variance estimation
The Nagelkerke scale normalization of R² differences provides comparability across continuous, binary, and survival outcomes
Multiplicative margins of error (e.g., 1.1) indicate that 95% CI width should not exceed a factor of 1.1 on the ratio scale for point estimate
User specified shrinkage ≥ 0.90, meaning adjusted R² should be ≥ 0.90 × apparent R²; this addresses overfitting penalty
Outcome mean multiplicative margin of error 1.1 constrains the 95% CI around the mean outcome estimate
Residual SD multiplicative margin of error 1.1 constrains precision of error variance (σ²) estimation through its square root

answer.summary: The minimum total development sample size for a continuous prediction model using Riley criteria with pmsampsize 1.1.3 is **918 participants**. This sample size is driven by two binding constraints: (1) the shrinkage criterion requiring ≥0.90 (i.e., ≤10% overfitting penalty) with 918 participants achieving exactly 0.900 shrinkage, and (2) the intercept (outcome mean) margin of error criterion requiring precise estimation with 95% confidence interval (1.87, 1.93) and multiplicative MOE of 1.018. The design accommodates 25 candidate predictor parameters, yielding 36.72 subjects per parameter (SPP)—substantially above the guideline minimum of 15–20 SPP, supporting conservative control of model overfitting and stability under internal validation. Criteria 2 (R-squared difference ≤0.05) and Criteria 3 (residual SD precision) are comfortably met at reduced sample sizes (401 and 259 participants, respectively) but do not govern the final recommendation.
answer.method: Analytic calculation using pmsampsize version 1.1.3, implementing the Riley et al. (2018, 2020) framework for prediction model sample-size determination. The package applies ordinary least squares regression theory to compute sample-size requirements against four simultaneous criteria: (i) shrinkage of predictor effects (overfitting penalty), (ii) absolute difference between apparent and adjusted R-squared ≤ 0.05, (iii) precise estimation of residual standard deviation within multiplicative margin of error, and (iv) precise estimation of outcome mean (intercept) within multiplicative margin of error. All criteria are evaluated at 95% confidence. The binding sample size is the maximum across all four criteria-specific calculations.
assumptions: Continuous outcome modeled using ordinary least squares (OLS) linear regression with 25 candidate predictor parameters
Anticipated adjusted R-squared = 0.20 (conservative estimate from prior studies)
Outcome mean (intercept) = 1.9 units
Outcome standard deviation = 0.6 units
Minimum acceptable shrinkage = 0.90 (predictor effect coefficients shrink by ≤10% at internal validation)
Maximum acceptable absolute difference between apparent and adjusted R² = 0.05 (default pmsampsize assumption)
Multiplicative margin of error for intercept estimation = 1.1 (user-specified; achieved MOE = 1.018)
Multiplicative margin of error for residual SD = 1.1 (default pmsampsize assumption)
Confidence level = 95% (default pmsampsize assumption)
Internal validation only; shrinkage criterion based on sample data splitting (fit-test framework)
All 25 predictors are linear main terms without interaction or polynomial terms requiring additional parameters
limitations: pmsampsize 1.1.3 does not implement separate user inputs for the R-squared difference criterion or residual SD margin of error criterion; these use fixed defaults (0.05 and 1.1, respectively) without package-level override
Sample size is based on anticipated R-squared; actual performance depends on true predictor–outcome relationships in development data
The calculation assumes standard OLS assumptions (normality of errors conditional on predictors); violation may affect shrinkage and precision properties
Subjects per predictor (SPP = 36.72) is calculable but pmsampsize does not expose intermediate SPP targets; sample size is determined by criterion binding constraints

The intercept multiplicative MOE achieved (1.018) is substantially conservative relative to the 1.1 target, driven by the shrinkage criterion taking precedence; residual SD and R-squared difference criteria are not binding
No adjustment for anticipated model selection, missing data, or exclusions; reported sample size is intended for analysis-ready development cohort
External validity and transportability of the fitted model to new populations are not addressed by sample-size calculation alone

# Install and load pmsampsize 1.1.3
if (!requireNamespace("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize")
}
library(pmsampsize)

# Confirm package version
pkg_version <- packageVersion("pmsampsize")
cat("pmsampsize version:", as.character(pkg_version), "\n\n")

# User-specified parameters for continuous prediction model
p <- 25                        # Number of candidate predictors
r2 <- 0.20                     # Anticipated adjusted R-squared
outcome_mean <- 1.9            # Outcome mean
outcome_sd <- 0.6              # Outcome standard deviation
shrinkage_target <- 0.90       # Minimum acceptable shrinkage
rsq_diff_max <- 0.05           # Maximum |apparent R^2 - adjusted R^2| on Nagelkerke scale
residual_sd_moe <- 1.1         # Residual SD multiplicative margin of error
outcome_mean_moe <- 1.1        # Outcome mean multiplicative margin of error
intercept_moe <- 1.1           # Intercept multiplicative margin of error
confidence <- 0.95             # Confidence level (default, explicit)

# Call pmsampsize for continuous outcome
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "c",                  # continuous outcome
  param = "Rp",                # Planning for R-squared (adjusted)
  r2 = r2,                     # Anticipated adjusted R-squared
  rcs = FALSE,                 # No restricted cubic splines (linear model)
  p = p,                       # Number of candidate predictors
  shrinkage = shrinkage_target,# Minimum acceptable shrinkage
  rsq_diff_max = rsq_diff_max, # Max absolute R^2 difference
  sd = outcome_sd,             # Outcome standard deviation
  mean = outcome_mean,         # Outcome mean
  mmoe = outcome_mean_moe,     # Mean multiplicative margin of error
  smmoe = residual_sd_moe,     # Residual SD multiplicative margin of error
  imoe = intercept_moe         # Intercept multiplicative margin of error
)

# Extract and display results
cat("Riley Criteria for Continuous Prediction Model Development\n")
cat("==========================================================\n\n")
cat("Input Parameters:\n")
cat("  Number of candidate predictors (p):", p, "\n")
cat("  Anticipated adjusted R-squared:", r2, "\n")
cat("  Outcome mean:", outcome_mean, "\n")
cat("  Outcome SD:", outcome_sd, "\n")
cat("  Minimum acceptable shrinkage:", shrinkage_target, "\n")
cat("  Max |apparent - adjusted R^2| (Nagelkerke):", rsq_diff_max, "\n")
cat("  Residual SD multiplicative MOE:", residual_sd_moe, "\n")
cat("  Outcome mean multiplicative MOE:", outcome_mean_moe, "\n")
cat("  Intercept multiplicative MOE:", intercept_moe, "\n")
cat("  Confidence level:", confidence, "\n\n")

cat("Results from pmsampsize():\n")
print(result)

# Extract minimum sample size
min_n <- result$samp_size
cat("\n\nMinimum Total Sample Size (Development):", min_n, "participants\n")

# Return structured result
cat("\n\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(jsonlite::toJSON(
  list(
    results = list(
      list(metric = "sample_size", 
           value = min_n, 
           unit = "participants_total")
    )
  ),
  auto_unbox = TRUE,
  digits = 15
))

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

     A list including a matrix of calculated sample size requirements
     for each criteria defined under _'Details'_, and a series of
     vectors of parameters used in the calculations as well as the
     final recommended minimum sample size and number of events
     required for model development.

_ E_ x_ a_ m_ p_ l_ e_ s:

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

rsq <- 0.20                    # Anticipated adjusted R-squared
outcome_mean <- 1.9            # Outcome mean (intercept)

shrinkage_target <- 0.90       # Minimum acceptable shrinkage
mmoe <- 1.1                    # Multiplicative margin of error for intercept (default)

# Call pmsampsize for continuous outcome
# Arguments: type, rsquared, parameters, shrinkage, intercept (mean), sd, mmoe
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "c",                  # continuous outcome
  rsquared = rsq,              # Anticipated adjusted R-squared
  parameters = p,              # Number of candidate predictors
  shrinkage = shrinkage_target,# Minimum acceptable shrinkage
  intercept = outcome_mean,    # Outcome mean
  sd = outcome_sd,             # Outcome standard deviation
  mmoe = mmoe                  # Multiplicative margin of error for intercept
)

# Display results
cat("Riley Criteria for Continuous Prediction Model Development\n")
cat("==========================================================\n\n")

pmsampsize 1.1.3 analytic formulation (Riley et al.) used; implementation assumes standard OLS assumptions (normality of residuals conditional on predictors)
Sample size calculated to meet the most stringent binding constraint among shrinkage, R² difference, and margin-of-error criteria
scientific_notes: Riley et al. criteria for prediction model development balance overfitting (shrinkage criterion) against precision of intercept, outcome mean, and residual variance estimation
The Nagelkerke scale normalization of R² differences provides comparability across continuous, binary, and survival outcomes
Multiplicative margins of error (e.g., 1.1) indicate that 95% CI width should not exceed a factor of 1.1 on the ratio scale for point estimate
User specified shrinkage ≥ 0.90, meaning adjusted R² should be ≥ 0.90 × apparent R²; this addresses overfitting penalty
Outcome mean multiplicative margin of error 1.1 constrains the 95% CI around the mean outcome estimate
Residual SD multiplicative margin of error 1.1 constrains precision of error variance (σ²) estimation through its square root

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development

          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

# Evidence e1; success=false

# Install and load pmsampsize 1.1.3
if (!requireNamespace("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize")
}
library(pmsampsize)

# Confirm package version
pkg_version <- packageVersion("pmsampsize")
cat("pmsampsize version:", as.character(pkg_version), "\n\n")

# User-specified parameters for continuous prediction model
p <- 25                        # Number of candidate predictors
r2 <- 0.20                     # Anticipated adjusted R-squared
outcome_mean <- 1.9            # Outcome mean
outcome_sd <- 0.6              # Outcome standard deviation
shrinkage_target <- 0.90       # Minimum acceptable shrinkage
rsq_diff_max <- 0.05           # Maximum |apparent R^2 - adjusted R^2| on Nagelkerke scale
residual_sd_moe <- 1.1         # Residual SD multiplicative margin of error
outcome_mean_moe <- 1.1        # Outcome mean multiplicative margin of error
intercept_moe <- 1.1           # Intercept multiplicative margin of error
confidence <- 0.95             # Confidence level (default, explicit)

# Call pmsampsize for continuous outcome
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "c",                  # continuous outcome
  param = "Rp",                # Planning for R-squared (adjusted)
  r2 = r2,                     # Anticipated adjusted R-squared
  rcs = FALSE,                 # No restricted cubic splines (linear model)
  p = p,                       # Number of candidate predictors
  shrinkage = shrinkage_target,# Minimum acceptable shrinkage
  rsq_diff_max = rsq_diff_max, # Max absolute R^2 difference
  sd = outcome_sd,             # Outcome standard deviation
  mean = outcome_mean,         # Outcome mean
  mmoe = outcome_mean_moe,     # Mean multiplicative margin of error
  smmoe = residual_sd_moe,     # Residual SD multiplicative margin of error
  imoe = intercept_moe         # Intercept multiplicative margin of error
)

# Extract and display results
cat("Riley Criteria for Continuous Prediction Model Development\n")
cat("==========================================================\n\n")
cat("Input Parameters:\n")
cat("  Number of candidate predictors (p):", p, "\n")
cat("  Anticipated adjusted R-squared:", r2, "\n")
cat("  Outcome mean:", outcome_mean, "\n")
cat("  Outcome SD:", outcome_sd, "\n")
cat("  Minimum acceptable shrinkage:", shrinkage_target, "\n")
cat("  Max |apparent - adjusted R^2| (Nagelkerke):", rsq_diff_max, "\n")
cat("  Residual SD multiplicative MOE:", residual_sd_moe, "\n")
cat("  Outcome mean multiplicative MOE:", outcome_mean_moe, "\n")
cat("  Intercept multiplicative MOE:", intercept_moe, "\n")
cat("  Confidence level:", confidence, "\n\n")

cat("Results from pmsampsize():\n")
print(result)

# Extract minimum sample size
min_n <- result$samp_size
cat("\n\nMinimum Total Sample Size (Development):", min_n, "participants\n")

# Return structured result
cat("\n\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(jsonlite::toJSON(
  list(
    results = list(
      list(metric = "sample_size", 
           value = min_n, 
           unit = "participants_total")
    )
  ),
  auto_unbox = TRUE,
  digits = 15
))

function (type, nagrsquared = NA, csrsquared = NA, rsquared = NA, parameters,

pmsampsize             package:pmsampsize              R Documentation

_ p_ m_ s_ a_ m_ p_ s_ i_ z_ e - _ S_ a_ m_ p_ l_ e _ S_ i_ z_ e _ f_ o_ r _ D_ e_ v_ e_ l_ o_ p_ m_ e_ n_ t _ o_ f _ a _ P_ r_ e_ d_ i_ c_ t_ i_ o_ n _ M_ o_ d_ e_ l

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,
       rsquared = NA,
       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,
       prevalence = NA,
       cstatistic = NA,
       seed = 123456,
       rate = NA,
       timepoint = NA,
       meanfup = NA,
       intercept = NA,
       sd = NA,
       mmoe = 1.1
     )
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     A list including a matrix of calculated sample size requirements
     for each criteria defined under _'Details'_, and a series of
     vectors of parameters used in the calculations as well as the
     final recommended minimum sample size and number of events
     required for model development.

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.

     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years

                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)

answer.summary: For a balanced one-way fixed effects ANOVA with 3 independent normal groups, common variance, and population eta-squared = 0.06, the minimum integer sample size per group yielding 80% power for the omnibus F test at α = 0.05 is **52 participants per group** (total N = 156). This design achieves an actual power of 80.56%, exceeding the 80% target. The preceding design with n = 51 per group yields only 79.73% power, falling below the target.
answer.method: Sample size inversion via pwr::pwr.anova.test (R package pwr v1.3-0) using non-central F distribution with effect size conversion η² = 0.06 → Cohen's f = √[η²/(1−η²)] = 0.2526. Binary search identified minimum integer n per group satisfying achieved power ≥ 80%. Test specification: omnibus F(k−1, N−k) with upper-tail rejection region; non-centrality parameter λ = √(N·f²) where N = n·k = total sample size.

Balanced allocation: equal n per group optimizes power for equal variance conditions

limitations: Sample size applies only to the omnibus test; no correction for multiple post-hoc comparisons
Calculation assumes no attrition or missing data; realistic studies may require inflation
Power is symmetric only under normality and equal variances; robustness to violations not assessed

# One-way ANOVA sample size calculation
# Target: 80% power, alpha = 0.05, eta-squared = 0.06, k = 3 groups

# Install pwr package if needed for ANOVA power calculations
if (!require("pwr", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pwr", repos = "http://cran.r-project.org")
}
library(pwr)

# Parameters
alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.80
eta_sq <- 0.06
k_groups <- 3

# Convert eta-squared to Cohen's f
# Cohen's f = sqrt(eta_sq / (1 - eta_sq))
# This is the effect size measure used by pwr package for ANOVA
f_effect <- sqrt(eta_sq / (1 - eta_sq))

cat("Effect size parameters:\n")
cat("Population eta-squared (η²):", eta_sq, "\n")
cat("Cohen's f:", f_effect, "\n")
cat("Number of groups (k):", k_groups, "\n")
cat("Significance level (α):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n\n")

# Search for minimum n per group that achieves target power
# Start with a reasonable range
n_min <- 1
n_max <- 500
tolerance <- 1e-6

# Use binary search to find the minimum n
while (n_max - n_min > 1) {
  n_mid <- ceiling((n_min + n_max) / 2)
  
  # Calculate power for this n using pwr.anova.test
  result <- pwr.anova.test(
    k = k_groups,
    n = n_mid,
    f = f_effect,
    sig.level = alpha
  )
  
  if (result$power >= target_power) {
    n_max <- n_mid
  } else {
    n_min <- n_mid
  }
}

# n_max is now the minimum integer n that achieves target power
n_optimal <- n_max

# Verify power at optimal n and preceding design
power_optimal <- pwr.anova.test(
  k = k_groups,
  n = n_optimal,
  f = f_effect,
  sig.level = alpha
)$power

power_preceding <- pwr.anova.test(
  k = k_groups,
  n = n_optimal - 1,
  f = f_effect,
  sig.level = alpha
)$power

cat("Sample size search results:\n")
cat("Minimum n per group meeting 80% power:", n_optimal, "\n")
cat("Total participants:", n_optimal * k_groups, "\n\n")

cat("Power verification:\n")
cat("Power at n =", n_optimal, ":", format(power_optimal, digits = 6), "\n")
cat("Power at n =", n_optimal - 1, ":", format(power_preceding, digits = 6), "\n\n")

# Additional design confirmation
cat("Design summary:\n")
cat("- Hypothesis: H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ vs. H₁: at least one mean differs\n")
cat("- Test: Omnibus F-test (upper-tail), α = ", alpha, "\n")
cat("- Groups: ", k_groups, " independent normal groups\n")
cat("- Assumption: Homogeneous variance (common σ²)\n")
cat("- Allocation: Balanced (n per group)\n")
cat("- Effect size: η² = ", eta_sq, " → Cohen's f = ", format(f_effect, digits = 6), "\n")

# Compute non-centrality parameter for documentation
lambda <- sqrt(n_optimal * k_groups * f_effect^2)
cat("- Non-centrality parameter λ at optimal n:", format(lambda, digits = 6), "\n\n")

# Store results for output
results <- data.frame(
  metric = "sample_size",
  value = n_optimal,
  unit = "participants_per_group",
  achieved_power = power_optimal,
  preceding_power = power_preceding
)

cat("FINAL RESULT:\n")
print(results)

# Independent verification of the one-way ANOVA sample size calculation
# Using alternative methodology and cross-checking critical elements

library(stats)
library(pwr)

# Study parameters
k <- 3  # number of groups
alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.80
eta_squared <- 0.06

cat("=== INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION ===\n\n")
cat("Study Design: Balanced one-way fixed effects ANOVA\n")
cat("H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ vs. H₁: not all means equal (omnibus test)\n")
cat("Parameters: k = ", k, ", α = ", alpha, ", target power = ", target_power, "\n")
cat("Population η² = ", eta_squared, "\n\n")

# Step 1: Convert η² to Cohen's f using the standard formula
# The relationship is: η² = f² / (1 + f²)
# Solving for f: f = √[η² / (1 - η²)]
f_cohen <- sqrt(eta_squared / (1 - eta_squared))
cat("Step 1: Effect Size Conversion\n")
cat("Cohen's f = √[η² / (1 - η²)] = √[", eta_squared, " / ", (1-eta_squared), "]\n")
cat("Cohen's f = ", format(f_cohen, digits = 10), "\n\n")

# Step 2: Manually verify the pwr.anova.test calculation
# The non-central F distribution uses non-centrality parameter:
# λ = √(N·f²) where N = n·k is the total sample size
cat("Step 2: Non-centrality Parameter Formula\n")
cat("λ = √(N·f²) = √(n·k·f²)\n\n")

# Step 3: Search for minimum n that achieves 80% power
# Method: Direct calculation at candidate values
n_candidates <- 50:55

cat("Step 3: Power Calculation at Candidate Sample Sizes\n")
cat(sprintf("%10s %12s %15s\n", "n per group", "Total N", "Power"))
cat(paste(rep("-", 40), collapse=""), "\n")

power_results <- data.frame()
for (n_test in n_candidates) {
  N_total <- n_test * k
  df1 <- k - 1
  df2 <- N_total - k
  lambda <- sqrt(N_total * f_cohen^2)
  
  # Critical F value under null hypothesis
  f_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df1, df2)
  
  # Power: P(F > f_crit) under non-central F distribution
  power <- 1 - pf(f_crit, df1, df2, ncp = lambda)
  
  cat(sprintf("%10d %12d %15.6f\n", n_test, N_total, power))
  
  power_results <- rbind(power_results, data.frame(
    n = n_test,
    N_total = N_total,
    power = power
  ))
}

cat("\n")

# Step 4: Identify minimum n meeting target power
meets_target <- power_results$power >= target_power
if (any(meets_target)) {
  min_n_idx <- which(meets_target)[1]
  min_n <- power_results$n[min_n_idx]
  min_power <- power_results$power[min_n_idx]
  
  cat("Step 4: Minimum Sample Size\n")
  cat("Minimum n per group: ", min_n, "\n")
  cat("Total participants: ", min_n * k, "\n")
  cat("Achieved power: ", format(min_power, digits = 8), "\n\n")
  
  # Verify preceding design
  if (min_n_idx > 1) {
    prev_n <- power_results$n[min_n_idx - 1]
    prev_power <- power_results$power[min_n_idx - 1]
    cat("Preceding design (n = ", prev_n, "): power = ", 
        format(prev_power, digits = 8), "\n")
    cat("Difference: ", format(min_power - prev_power, digits = 8), "\n\n")
  }
} else {
  cat("ERROR: No candidate n meets target power\n")
}

# Step 5: Cross-check with pwr package
cat("Step 5: Cross-check with pwr::pwr.anova.test\n")
pwr_check <- pwr.anova.test(k = k, n = min_n, f = f_cohen, sig.level = alpha)
cat("pwr package result for n = ", min_n, ": power = ", 
    format(pwr_check$power, digits = 8), "\n")
cat("Difference from manual calculation: ", 
    format(abs(pwr_check$power - min_power), digits = 2e-10), "\n\n")

# Step 6: Verify that n-1 does not meet target
pwr_prev <- pwr.anova.test(k = k, n = min_n - 1, f = f_cohen, sig.level = alpha)
cat("Step 6: Verify Minimum Property\n")
cat("n = ", min_n - 1, ": power = ", format(pwr_prev$power, digits = 8),
    " (BELOW 0.80) ✓\n")
cat("n = ", min_n, ": power = ", format(pwr_check$power, digits = 8),
    " (MEETS 0.80) ✓\n\n")

# Step 7: Final confirmation
cat("=== FINAL RESULT ===\n")
cat("Sample size per group: ", min_n, "\n")
cat("Total participants: ", min_n * k, "\n")
cat("Achieved power: ", format(pwr_check$power, digits = 6), "\n")
cat("Status: MINIMUM INTEGER n CONFIRMED\n\n")

# Output in required format
POWER_AGENT_RESULT=list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = min_n, unit = "participants_per_group"),
    list(metric = "achieved_power", value = round(pwr_check$power, 6), unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "preceding_design_power", value = round(pwr_prev$power, 6), unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "total_participants", value = min_n * k, unit = "count")
  )
)

cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=", jsonlite::toJSON(POWER_AGENT_RESULT, auto_unbox=TRUE, digits=15), sep="")

function (k = NULL, n = NULL, f = NULL, sig.level = 0.05, power = NULL) 
{
    if (sum(sapply(list(k, n, f, power, sig.level), is.null)) != 
        1) 
        stop("exactly one of k, n, f, power, and sig.level must be NULL")
    if (!is.null(f)) {
        if (is.character(f)) 
            f <- cohen.ES(test = "anov", size = f)$effect.size
        if (any(f < 0)) 
            stop("f must be positive")
    }
    if (!is.null(k) && any(k < 2)) 
        stop("number of groups must be at least 2")
    if (!is.null(n) && any(n < 2)) 
        stop("number of observations in each group must be at least 2")
    if (!is.null(sig.level) && !is.numeric(sig.level) || any(0 > 
        sig.level | sig.level > 1)) 
        stop(sQuote("sig.level"), " must be numeric in [0, 1]")
    if (!is.null(power) && !is.numeric(power) || any(0 > power | 
        power > 1)) 
        stop(sQuote("power"), " must be numeric in [0, 1]")
    p.body <- quote({
        lambda <- k * n * f^2
        pf(qf(sig.level, k - 1, (n - 1) * k, lower = FALSE), 
            k - 1, (n - 1) * k, lambda, lower = FALSE)
    })
    if (is.null(power)) 
        power <- eval(p.body)
    else if (is.null(k)) 
        k <- uniroot(function(k) eval(p.body) - power, c(2 + 
            1e-10, 100))$root
    else if (is.null(n)) 
        n <- uniroot(function(n) eval(p.body) - power, c(2 + 
            1e-10, 1e+09))$root
    else if (is.null(f)) 
        f <- uniroot(function(f) eval(p.body) - power, c(1e-07, 
            1e+07))$root
    else if (is.null(sig.level)) 
        sig.level <- uniroot(function(sig.level) eval(p.body) - 
            power, c(1e-10, 1 - 1e-10))$root
    else stop("internal error")
    NOTE <- "n is number in each group"
    METHOD <- "Balanced one-way analysis of variance power calculation"
    structure(list(k = k, n = n, f = f, sig.level = sig.level, 
        power = power, note = NOTE, method = METHOD), class = "power.htest")
}

plan.estimand: Omnibus F-test effect size in one-way fixed effects ANOVA with 3 independent normal groups and common variance
plan.hypothesis: H0: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ (all group means equal); H1: at least one group mean differs
assumptions: Three independent normal groups
Homogeneity of variance (equal population variances across groups)
Fixed effects model (groups represent all levels of interest, not sampled from a larger population)
Observations are independent within and between groups
Population eta-squared = 0.06 represents the true effect size
scientific_notes: Eta-squared (η²) = 0.06 is a medium effect size by convention, representing 6% of total variance explained by group membership
Omnibus F test is upper-tail (one-sided) testing for any difference among means
Balanced design (equal n per group) is computationally efficient and optimal for equal variance conditions
Sample size will be inverted to find the minimum integer n per group meeting 80% power threshold
Non-centrality parameter λ depends on sample size, number of groups, and effect size

# One-way ANOVA sample size calculation
# Target: 80% power, alpha = 0.05, eta-squared = 0.06, k = 3 groups

# Install pwr package if needed for ANOVA power calculations
if (!require("pwr", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pwr", repos = "http://cran.r-project.org")
}
library(pwr)

# Parameters
alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.80
eta_sq <- 0.06
k_groups <- 3

# Convert eta-squared to Cohen's f
# Cohen's f = sqrt(eta_sq / (1 - eta_sq))
# This is the effect size measure used by pwr package for ANOVA
f_effect <- sqrt(eta_sq / (1 - eta_sq))

cat("Effect size parameters:\n")
cat("Population eta-squared (η²):", eta_sq, "\n")
cat("Cohen's f:", f_effect, "\n")
cat("Number of groups (k):", k_groups, "\n")
cat("Significance level (α):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n\n")

# Search for minimum n per group that achieves target power
# Start with a reasonable range
n_min <- 1
n_max <- 500
tolerance <- 1e-6

# Use binary search to find the minimum n
while (n_max - n_min > 1) {
  n_mid <- ceiling((n_min + n_max) / 2)
  
  # Calculate power for this n using pwr.anova.test
  result <- pwr.anova.test(
    k = k_groups,
    n = n_mid,
    f = f_effect,
    sig.level = alpha
  )
  
  if (result$power >= target_power) {
    n_max <- n_mid
  } else {
    n_min <- n_mid
  }
}

# n_max is now the minimum integer n that achieves target power
n_optimal <- n_max

# Verify power at optimal n and preceding design
power_optimal <- pwr.anova.test(
  k = k_groups,
  n = n_optimal,
  f = f_effect,
  sig.level = alpha
)$power

power_preceding <- pwr.anova.test(
  k = k_groups,
  n = n_optimal - 1,
  f = f_effect,
  sig.level = alpha
)$power

cat("Sample size search results:\n")
cat("Minimum n per group meeting 80% power:", n_optimal, "\n")
cat("Total participants:", n_optimal * k_groups, "\n\n")

cat("Power verification:\n")
cat("Power at n =", n_optimal, ":", format(power_optimal, digits = 6), "\n")
cat("Power at n =", n_optimal - 1, ":", format(power_preceding, digits = 6), "\n\n")

# Additional design confirmation
cat("Design summary:\n")
cat("- Hypothesis: H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ vs. H₁: at least one mean differs\n")
cat("- Test: Omnibus F-test (upper-tail), α = ", alpha, "\n")
cat("- Groups: ", k_groups, " independent normal groups\n")
cat("- Assumption: Homogeneous variance (common σ²)\n")
cat("- Allocation: Balanced (n per group)\n")
cat("- Effect size: η² = ", eta_sq, " → Cohen's f = ", format(f_effect, digits = 6), "\n")

# Compute non-centrality parameter for documentation
lambda <- sqrt(n_optimal * k_groups * f_effect^2)
cat("- Non-centrality parameter λ at optimal n:", format(lambda, digits = 6), "\n\n")

# Store results for output
results <- data.frame(
  metric = "sample_size",
  value = n_optimal,
  unit = "participants_per_group",
  achieved_power = power_optimal,
  preceding_power = power_preceding
)

cat("FINAL RESULT:\n")
print(results)

# Method 1: Using pwr package (primary)
power_pwr <- pwr.anova.test(k = k, n = n, f = f_effect, sig.level = alpha)

cat("   f = ", format(f_effect, digits = 8), "\n")
cat("   n = ", n, " per group\n")
cat("   N total = ", n*k, "\n")
cat("   Power = ", format(power_pwr$power, digits = 8), "\n\n")

# The pwr package uses the non-central F distribution with
# non-centrality parameter: lambda = sqrt(n * k * f^2)
# But we need to verify this is the correct lambda parameterization

cat("2. Non-centrality parameter check:\n")
lambda_v1 <- sqrt(n * k * f_effect^2)
cat("   λ (using √(N·f²)) = ", format(lambda_v1, digits = 8), "\n")

# Some sources define lambda differently for ANOVA
# Let's check the relationship: for balanced ANOVA,
# λ = sqrt(sum of squared effects / variance)
# λ = sqrt(n * Σ(μi - μ_bar)² / σ²)
# which relates to f as: f² = Σ(μi - μ_bar)² / (k*σ²)

# For k=3 groups with η² = 0.06:
# This implies the effect accounts for 6% of variance
# The relationship is: f = √[η²/(1-η²)] which we already have

cat("   λ (alternative parameterization) = n·k·f / √k = ", 
    format(n*k*f_effect/sqrt(k), digits = 8), "\n")

# Verify against degrees of freedom

df2 <- n*k - k  # denominator (within groups)

cat("Study Design: Balanced one-way fixed effects ANOVA\n")
cat("H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ vs. H₁: not all means equal (omnibus test)\n")
cat("Parameters: k = ", k, ", α = ", alpha, ", target power = ", target_power, "\n")
cat("Population η² = ", eta_squared, "\n\n")

# Step 1: Convert η² to Cohen's f using the standard formula
# The relationship is: η² = f² / (1 + f²)
# Solving for f: f = √[η² / (1 - η²)]
f_cohen <- sqrt(eta_squared / (1 - eta_squared))
cat("Step 1: Effect Size Conversion\n")
cat("Cohen's f = √[η² / (1 - η²)] = √[", eta_squared, " / ", (1-eta_squared), "]\n")
cat("Cohen's f = ", format(f_cohen, digits = 10), "\n\n")

# Step 2: Manually verify the pwr.anova.test calculation
# The non-central F distribution uses non-centrality parameter:
# λ = √(N·f²) where N = n·k is the total sample size
cat("Step 2: Non-centrality Parameter Formula\n")
cat("λ = √(N·f²) = √(n·k·f²)\n\n")

# Step 3: Search for minimum n that achieves 80% power
# Method: Direct calculation at candidate values
n_candidates <- 50:55

cat("Step 3: Power Calculation at Candidate Sample Sizes\n")
cat(sprintf("%10s %12s %15s\n", "n per group", "Total N", "Power"))
cat(paste(rep("-", 40), collapse=""), "\n")

power_results <- data.frame()
for (n_test in n_candidates) {
  N_total <- n_test * k
  df1 <- k - 1
  df2 <- N_total - k
  lambda <- sqrt(N_total * f_cohen^2)
  
  # Critical F value under null hypothesis
  f_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df1, df2)
  
  # Power: P(F > f_crit) under non-central F distribution
  power <- 1 - pf(f_crit, df1, df2, ncp = lambda)
  
  cat(sprintf("%10d %12d %15.6f\n", n_test, N_total, power))
  
  power_results <- rbind(power_results, data.frame(
    n = n_test,
    N_total = N_total,
    power = power
  ))
}

cat("\n")

# Step 4: Identify minimum n meeting target power
meets_target <- power_results$power >= target_power
if (any(meets_target)) {
  min_n_idx <- which(meets_target)[1]
  min_n <- power_results$n[min_n_idx]
  min_power <- power_results$power[min_n_idx]
  
  cat("Step 4: Minimum Sample Size\n")
  cat("Minimum n per group: ", min_n, "\n")
  cat("Total participants: ", min_n * k, "\n")
  cat("Achieved power: ", format(min_power, digits = 8), "\n\n")
  
  # Verify preceding design
  if (min_n_idx > 1) {
    prev_n <- power_results$n[min_n_idx - 1]
    prev_power <- power_results$power[min_n_idx - 1]
    cat("Preceding design (n = ", prev_n, "): power = ", 
        format(prev_power, digits = 8), "\n")
    cat("Difference: ", format(min_power - prev_power, digits = 8), "\n\n")
  }
} else {
  cat("ERROR: No candidate n meets target power\n")
}

# Step 5: Cross-check with pwr package
cat("Step 5: Cross-check with pwr::pwr.anova.test\n")
pwr_check <- pwr.anova.test(k = k, n = min_n, f = f_cohen, sig.level = alpha)
cat("pwr package result for n = ", min_n, ": power = ", 
    format(pwr_check$power, digits = 8), "\n")
cat("Difference from manual calculation: ", 
    format(abs(pwr_check$power - min_power), digits = 2e-10), "\n\n")

# Step 6: Verify that n-1 does not meet target
pwr_prev <- pwr.anova.test(k = k, n = min_n - 1, f = f_cohen, sig.level = alpha)
cat("Step 6: Verify Minimum Property\n")
cat("n = ", min_n - 1, ": power = ", format(pwr_prev$power, digits = 8),
    " (BELOW 0.80) ✓\n")
cat("n = ", min_n, ": power = ", format(pwr_check$power, digits = 8),
    " (MEETS 0.80) ✓\n\n")

# Step 7: Final confirmation
cat("=== FINAL RESULT ===\n")
cat("Sample size per group: ", min_n, "\n")
cat("Total participants: ", min_n * k, "\n")
cat("Achieved power: ", format(pwr_check$power, digits = 6), "\n")
cat("Status: MINIMUM INTEGER n CONFIRMED\n\n")

# Output in required format
POWER_AGENT_RESULT=list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = min_n, unit = "participants_per_group"),
    list(metric = "achieved_power", value = round(pwr_check$power, 6), unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "preceding_design_power", value = round(pwr_prev$power, 6), unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "total_participants", value = min_n * k, unit = "count")
  )
)

cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=", jsonlite::toJSON(POWER_AGENT_RESULT, auto_unbox=TRUE, digits=15), sep="")

# Investigate the non-centrality parameter definition used by pwr package
# The issue may be in how λ is parameterized for the non-central F distribution

library(pwr)
library(stats)

k <- 3
alpha <- 0.05
eta_squared <- 0.06
n <- 52

f_cohen <- sqrt(eta_squared / (1 - eta_squared))
N_total <- n * k

cat("=== Investigation of Non-centrality Parameterization ===\n\n")

cat("Parameters:\n")
cat("  k = ", k, " groups\n")
cat("  n = ", n, " per group\n")
cat("  N (total) = ", N_total, "\n")
cat("  η² = ", eta_squared, "\n")
cat("  Cohen's f = ", format(f_cohen, digits = 10), "\n\n")

# Hypothesis test specifics
df1 <- k - 1
df2 <- N_total - k
f_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df1, df2)

cat("F-test degrees of freedom:\n")
cat("  df1 (numerator) = ", df1, "\n")
cat("  df2 (denominator) = ", df2, "\n")
cat("  F_critical (α=0.05) = ", format(f_crit, digits = 8), "\n\n")

# The pwr package uses a specific non-centrality definition
# For ANOVA, the non-central F distribution parameter can be defined as:
# λ = √(n·k·f²) (the form I used)
# But some sources and implementations use: λ = √(sum of squared standardized effects)

# Let's investigate what the pwr package actually uses
# by checking the source or behavior

cat("Investigation of non-centrality parameter definition:\n\n")

# The standard ANOVA non-centrality parameter for the F statistic is:
# λ² = Σ(μᵢ - μ_bar)² / σ² × n
# where the sum is over k groups

# For the parameterization using Cohen's f:
# f = √[Σ(μᵢ - μ_bar)² / (k·σ²)]
# So: Σ(μᵢ - μ_bar)² / σ² = k·f²

# Therefore: λ² = k·f² × n
# λ = √(k·n·f²) = √(k·N·f²/k) = √(N·f²) -- This matches my original formula

lambda_v1 <- sqrt(N_total * f_cohen^2)
cat("λ (using √(N·f²)) = ", format(lambda_v1, digits = 10), "\n")

# But the pwr documentation and some implementations may use a different convention
# Let's check by examining what parameter gives power close to 0.805564

# Try different parameterizations
cat("\nTesting different λ parameterizations:\n")
cat("λ value          Power achieved\n")
cat(paste(rep("-", 35), collapse=""), "\n")

# Test a range of lambda values to find which one gives ~0.806 power
for (lambda_test in seq(2.5, 4.5, by = 0.1)) {
  power_test <- 1 - pf(f_crit, df1, df2, ncp = lambda_test)
  cat(sprintf("%12.6f      %12.6f\n", lambda_test, power_test))
  
  if (abs(power_test - 0.805564) < 0.0001) {
    cat("  ^^^ MATCH FOUND ^^^\n")
  }
}

cat("\n")

# Also check the pwr package documentation parameterization
cat("According to pwr package documentation:\n")
cat("  pwr.anova.test uses the effect size parameter 'f' (Cohen's f)\n")
cat("  and computes power via non-central F distribution\n\n")

# Let me try an alternative lambda definition sometimes used:
# In some contexts, λ for F-test is defined as:
# λ² = n · Σ(μᵢ - μ_grand)² / σ²
# For balanced case with equal effects: this becomes λ = √(n · k · f²)

lambda_v2 <- sqrt(n * k * f_cohen^2)
cat("Alternative: λ (using √(n·k·f²)) = ", format(lambda_v2, digits = 10), "\n")

power_v2 <- 1 - pf(f_crit, df1, df2, ncp = lambda_v2)
cat("Power with λ = √(n·k·f²): ", format(power_v2, digits = 8), "\n\n")

# Now check what pwr.anova.test actually returns
pwr_result <- pwr.anova.test(k = k, n = n, f = f_cohen, sig.level = alpha)
cat("pwr.anova.test result: power = ", format(pwr_result$power, digits = 8), "\n\n")

# The issue might be that pwr uses a different internal calculation
# Let me check if it's the effect size metric itself
cat("=== Examining pwr source and documentation ===\n")
cat("The pwr package's pwr.anova.test function documentation states:\n")
cat("'f: effect size (Cohen's f coefficient)'\n\n")
cat("The non-centrality parameter λ in the pwr implementation should be:\n")
cat("λ = f × √(n × k)\n")

lambda_pwr <- f_cohen * sqrt(n * k)
cat("λ (pwr convention: f × √(n·k)) = ", format(lambda_pwr, digits = 10), "\n")

power_pwr_conv <- 1 - pf(f_crit, df1, df2, ncp = lambda_pwr)
cat("Power with this λ: ", format(power_pwr_conv, digits = 8), "\n\n")

# FOUND IT! The pwr package likely uses: λ = f × √(N) where N = n·k
# Let's verify
lambda_final <- f_cohen * sqrt(N_total)
cat("Final check: λ (using f × √(N)) = ", format(lambda_final, digits = 10), "\n")
power_final <- 1 - pf(f_crit, df1, df2, ncp = lambda_final)
cat("Power with λ = f × √(N): ", format(power_final, digits = 8), "\n\n")

if (abs(power_final - 0.805564) < 0.0001) {
  cat("✓ MATCH: The pwr package uses λ = f × √(N)\n")
}

# Evidence e1; success=true

# One-way ANOVA sample size calculation
# Target: 80% power, alpha = 0.05, eta-squared = 0.06, k = 3 groups

# Install pwr package if needed for ANOVA power calculations
if (!require("pwr", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pwr", repos = "http://cran.r-project.org")
}
library(pwr)

# Parameters
alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.80
eta_sq <- 0.06
k_groups <- 3

# Convert eta-squared to Cohen's f
# Cohen's f = sqrt(eta_sq / (1 - eta_sq))
# This is the effect size measure used by pwr package for ANOVA
f_effect <- sqrt(eta_sq / (1 - eta_sq))

cat("Effect size parameters:\n")
cat("Population eta-squared (η²):", eta_sq, "\n")
cat("Cohen's f:", f_effect, "\n")
cat("Number of groups (k):", k_groups, "\n")
cat("Significance level (α):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n\n")

# Search for minimum n per group that achieves target power
# Start with a reasonable range
n_min <- 1
n_max <- 500
tolerance <- 1e-6

# Use binary search to find the minimum n
while (n_max - n_min > 1) {
  n_mid <- ceiling((n_min + n_max) / 2)
  
  # Calculate power for this n using pwr.anova.test
  result <- pwr.anova.test(
    k = k_groups,
    n = n_mid,
    f = f_effect,
    sig.level = alpha
  )
  
  if (result$power >= target_power) {
    n_max <- n_mid
  } else {
    n_min <- n_mid
  }
}

# n_max is now the minimum integer n that achieves target power
n_optimal <- n_max

# Verify power at optimal n and preceding design
power_optimal <- pwr.anova.test(
  k = k_groups,
  n = n_optimal,
  f = f_effect,
  sig.level = alpha
)$power

power_preceding <- pwr.anova.test(
  k = k_groups,
  n = n_optimal - 1,
  f = f_effect,
  sig.level = alpha
)$power

cat("Sample size search results:\n")
cat("Minimum n per group meeting 80% power:", n_optimal, "\n")
cat("Total participants:", n_optimal * k_groups, "\n\n")

cat("Power verification:\n")
cat("Power at n =", n_optimal, ":", format(power_optimal, digits = 6), "\n")
cat("Power at n =", n_optimal - 1, ":", format(power_preceding, digits = 6), "\n\n")

# Additional design confirmation
cat("Design summary:\n")
cat("- Hypothesis: H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ vs. H₁: at least one mean differs\n")
cat("- Test: Omnibus F-test (upper-tail), α = ", alpha, "\n")
cat("- Groups: ", k_groups, " independent normal groups\n")
cat("- Assumption: Homogeneous variance (common σ²)\n")
cat("- Allocation: Balanced (n per group)\n")
cat("- Effect size: η² = ", eta_sq, " → Cohen's f = ", format(f_effect, digits = 6), "\n")

# Compute non-centrality parameter for documentation
lambda <- sqrt(n_optimal * k_groups * f_effect^2)
cat("- Non-centrality parameter λ at optimal n:", format(lambda, digits = 6), "\n\n")

# Store results for output
results <- data.frame(
  metric = "sample_size",
  value = n_optimal,
  unit = "participants_per_group",
  achieved_power = power_optimal,
  preceding_power = power_preceding
)

cat("FINAL RESULT:\n")
print(results)

k <- 3
alpha <- 0.05
n <- 52

f_effect <- sqrt(eta_sq / (1 - eta_sq))

# The pwr.anova.test function uses a specific power calculation method
# Let's examine what it's doing internally and verify

cat("=== Power Calculation Methodology ===\n\n")

# Method 1: Using pwr package (primary)
power_pwr <- pwr.anova.test(k = k, n = n, f = f_effect, sig.level = alpha)

cat("1. Using pwr::pwr.anova.test (non-central F distribution):\n")
cat("   f = ", format(f_effect, digits = 8), "\n")
cat("   n = ", n, " per group\n")
cat("   N total = ", n*k, "\n")
cat("   Power = ", format(power_pwr$power, digits = 8), "\n\n")

# The pwr package uses the non-central F distribution with
# non-centrality parameter: lambda = sqrt(n * k * f^2)
# But we need to verify this is the correct lambda parameterization

cat("2. Non-centrality parameter check:\n")
lambda_v1 <- sqrt(n * k * f_effect^2)
cat("   λ (using √(N·f²)) = ", format(lambda_v1, digits = 8), "\n")

# Some sources define lambda differently for ANOVA
# Let's check the relationship: for balanced ANOVA,
# λ = sqrt(sum of squared effects / variance)
# λ = sqrt(n * Σ(μi - μ_bar)² / σ²)
# which relates to f as: f² = Σ(μi - μ_bar)² / (k*σ²)

# For k=3 groups with η² = 0.06:
# This implies the effect accounts for 6% of variance
# The relationship is: f = √[η²/(1-η²)] which we already have

cat("   λ (alternative parameterization) = n·k·f / √k = ", 
    format(n*k*f_effect/sqrt(k), digits = 8), "\n")

# Verify against degrees of freedom
df1 <- k - 1  # numerator (between groups)
df2 <- n*k - k  # denominator (within groups)

cat("\n3. F-test degrees of freedom:\n")
cat("   df1 (between groups) = k - 1 = ", df1, "\n")
cat("   df2 (within groups) = N - k = ", df2, "\n")

# Critical F value
f_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df1, df2)
cat("   F_critical(2, 153, α=0.05) = ", format(f_crit, digits = 8), "\n\n")

cat("4. Power formula verification:\n")
cat("   The pwr package implementation computes:\n")
cat("   Power = P(F_{df1,df2}(λ) > F_crit)\n")
cat("   This is the correct formula for balanced one-way ANOVA.\n\n")

# Report achieved and preceding power
power_prev <- pwr.anova.test(k = k, n = n-1, f = f_effect, sig.level = alpha)

cat("=== Final Sample Size Result ===\n\n")
cat("Minimum n per group: ", n, "\n")
cat("Total participants: ", n*k, "\n")
cat("Power at n =", n, ":", format(power_pwr$power, digits = 6), "\n")
cat("Power at n =", n-1, ":", format(power_prev$power, digits = 6), "\n\n")
cat("✓ n = ", n, " exceeds target power of 0.80\n")

answer.summary: A one-sided one-sample t-test with H₀: μ = 0 vs. H₁: μ > 0 at significance level α = 0.05 requires **41 participants** to achieve 80% power when detecting a mean increase of 0.2 units with standard deviation 0.5 (Cohen's d = 0.4). Analytical calculation via the non-central t distribution yields achieved power of 80.86% at n = 41; the preceding design (n = 40) achieves 79.97% power. Monte Carlo verification with 10,000 simulations (seed 12345) confirms the result (simulated power 80.72%, 95% CI [79.95%, 81.49%], MCSE 0.003945).
answer.method: Analytical inversion of the non-central t distribution using the cumulative distribution function of the non-central t. Power for sample size n is P(t ≥ t_{1−α,n−1} | δ = d√n), where t_{1−α,n−1} is the upper α-quantile with n−1 degrees of freedom and δ = 0.4√n is the non-centrality parameter. Minimum sample size determined by grid search over integers n ∈ {2, …, 150}, selecting the smallest n where power ≥ 0.80. Achieved power and preceding design power computed analytically. Monte Carlo verification: 10,000 independent replications of data generation from N(0.2, 0.5²) with one-sided t-test rejection at α = 0.05 (seed 12345).

No missing data, attrition, or dropout during study
Participants are independent and identically distributed
Fixed sample size design with no interim analyses or adaptive features
Study will recruit exactly 41 participants and analyze all available data
limitations: Analytical power assumes normality; robustness to moderate departures is good at n = 41 but heavy tails or skewness may reduce actual power

Calculation does not account for missing data or dropout; if ≥8% attrition is expected, inflate sample size
One-sided test is appropriate only if direction of effect specified prospectively; deviation to two-sided testing reduces power from 80.9% to ~70%
Discrete rounding: continuous solution via inversion would be ~40.5; smallest integer is 41
